sections.h: Budget, resources and risks
sections.md:
**Budget.** List costs by category: people (internal time and contractors), equipment, software, travel, training, and contingency (often 10–15% for uncertain projects). Track **actual vs planned** spending monthly.

Example: hardware ₹9 lakh, installation ₹2 lakh, training ₹1.5 lakh, process consultant ₹3 lakh = ₹15.5 lakh; contingency ≈ 15% of 15.5 ≈ ₹2.3 lakh; total ≈ ₹17.8 lakh, within the ₹18 lakh budget.

**Resources.** People are usually the scarcest resource. Watch for over-allocation: the same IT engineer booked full-time on three projects in the same week. Agree availability with line managers in writing.

**Risks** are things that *might* happen; **issues** are things that *have* happened. Manage risks before they become issues.

**A risk register** lists each risk with likelihood, impact, owner and response:

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Response | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hardware delivery delayed | Medium | High | Order early; identify backup vendor | IT |
| Staff resist new process | Medium | Medium | Involve staff in design; champions | Branch head |
| Power cuts during launch | Low | High | UPS for token machines | Facilities |
| Monsoon flooding delays installation | Low | Medium | Schedule install before June | PM |

**Four response strategies:** **avoid** (change the plan to remove the risk), **reduce** (make it less likely or less harmful), **transfer** (insurance, contract clauses) and **accept** (with a contingency plan).

Review the register every week or two. New risks appear; old ones close.

check.q: Buying insurance against equipment damage is an example of which risk response?
check.why: Insurance shifts the financial impact of the risk to another party.

sections.h: Waterfall, agile and hybrid
sections.md:
Two broad approaches dominate.

**Waterfall (plan-driven):** define requirements, design, build, test and deploy in sequence. Best when requirements are clear and stable and changes are expensive — constructing a building, installing hardware, regulatory projects.

**Agile (iterative):** deliver in short cycles (often 1–4 weeks, called sprints in the Scrum method), get feedback, adjust. Best when requirements are uncertain or likely to change — software, new products, marketing experiments. Popular agile practices include:
- A prioritised **backlog** of work.
- **Sprint planning**, daily **stand-ups**, **reviews** (show working results) and **retrospectives** (improve how we work).
- **Kanban boards** with columns like *To do → In progress → Done*, and limits on work in progress.

**Hybrid** approaches are common: the service-centre project might plan the hardware installation in waterfall style while designing the customer flow iteratively with front-desk staff.

| | Waterfall | Agile |
|---|---|---|
| Requirements | Fixed early | Evolve |
| Delivery | One big release | Frequent small releases |
| Change | Controlled, costly | Expected, welcomed |
| Best for | Stable, well-understood work | Uncertain, innovative work |

The right approach depends on the work, not on fashion.

check.q: Which project is best suited to an agile approach?
options: A new mobile app where user needs are uncertain
check.why: Uncertain requirements benefit from short cycles of building, feedback and adjustment.

sections.h: Tracking, communicating and handling change
sections.md:
**Track progress weekly** against milestones, budget and risks. A simple **RAG status** (Red, Amber, Green) is widely used:
- **Green:** on track.
- **Amber:** at risk; action under way.
- **Red:** off track; needs a decision or help.

Be honest. "Watermelon projects" — green outside, red inside — destroy trust when the truth surfaces. Amber early is far better than red late.

**A one-page weekly status report:**
> **Overall:** Amber — hardware delayed 1 week.
> **Done:** process design approved; vendor signed.
> **Next:** hardware delivery (12 May), training starts (15 May).
> **Risks/issues:** delivery delay; mitigation: install over a weekend.
> **Decisions needed:** approve ₹40,000 weekend installation cost.

**Communication plan:** who needs what information, how often, in what format — sponsor weekly summary, team daily stand-up, staff monthly newsletter, customers a notice two weeks before go-live.

**Scope creep** — small additions that pile up ("Can we also add SMS alerts?") — is a leading cause of overruns. Use a simple **change control** process: record the request, assess impact on time, cost and risk, get the sponsor's decision, update the plan. Saying *"Yes, and it will add two weeks and ₹1.2 lakh — shall we?"* is far better than a silent yes.

check.q: A 'watermelon project' is one that:
options: Reports green but is actually in trouble
check.why: It looks green on the outside while being red inside, which hides problems until too late.

sections.h: Closing the project and learning
sections.md:
Projects need a proper end, or they drift into an endless half-finished state.

**Closure steps:**
1. **Confirm acceptance** — the sponsor and users agree deliverables meet the success criteria.
2. **Hand over to operations** — who will run, maintain and support the new system? Train them, document it, agree service levels.
3. **Close contracts and accounts** — final vendor payments, release unused budget.
4. **Release people** back to their teams, with thanks and recognition.
5. **Hold a lessons-learned review** — what went well, what didn't, what we'd do differently. Keep it blameless and specific.
6. **Measure benefits later** — some results (like wait times) need weeks or months to show.
7. **Celebrate** — even a team lunch matters.

**Lessons are worthless unless used.** Store them where the next project team will find them, and read the last project's lessons before starting a new one.

> **Did you know?** The Delhi Metro's first phase is often cited as a well-run Indian infrastructure project, credited with finishing ahead of schedule — commentators point to strong leadership, clear accountability and disciplined planning.

check.q: Why hand over to operations formally at project close?
options: So someone is clearly responsible for running and supporting the result
Because the team wants a holiday
check.why: Without a clear handover, new systems lack owners and support, and benefits fade.

rd-engineering-bridges.title: How Bridges Stand
rd-engineering-bridges.subtitle: Tension, compression and the clever shapes that carry trains across rivers and roads across the sea

sections.h: A train over the Chenab
sections.md:
High in the mountains of Jammu and Kashmir, a train rolls across a steel arch that springs from one side of the Chenab gorge to the other. The rails run about 359 metres above the river — higher than the Eiffel Tower's main structure. Winds howl through the valley; the region is seismically active; temperatures swing from summer heat to winter freezes. And yet the bridge, opened to rail traffic in 2025, carries trains of hundreds of tonnes as if they weighed nothing.

How? Every bridge, from a plank over a village stream to the Chenab arch, solves the same problem: **getting loads safely from the deck into the ground**. The deck carries cars, trains and people; their weight must travel through the structure to the supports and finally into rock or soil. Engineers choose shapes that send those forces along paths the materials can handle.

In this read we'll follow the forces:

1. Loads — what a bridge must carry.
2. Tension, compression, bending and shear.
3. Materials: stone, steel, concrete and prestressing.
4. The beam bridge and the truss.
5. The arch.
6. Suspension and cable-stayed bridges.
7. Foundations, wind, earthquakes and fatigue.
8. Famous Indian bridges and how engineers keep bridges safe.

check.q: The basic job of every bridge structure is to:
options: Carry loads from the deck safely into the ground
check.why: All bridge forms are different ways of routing loads from the deck through the structure to the foundations.

sections.h: Loads: what a bridge must carry
sections.md:
Engineers list every force a bridge might face, then design with a safety margin.

- **Dead load** — the bridge's own weight: deck, beams, railings, road surface. Often the largest load on big bridges.
- **Live load** — traffic: cars, trucks, trains, people. It moves and varies. Indian road bridges are designed using standard vehicle loadings set out in Indian Roads Congress (IRC) codes; railway bridges follow Indian Railways standards.
- **Impact** — moving loads bounce and jolt, so designers increase live loads by an impact factor.
- **Wind** — pushes sideways and can make long, light bridges vibrate.
- **Temperature** — steel and concrete expand when hot and contract when cold. A 1-kilometre steel deck can change length by around 0.4 metres between a cold winter night and a hot summer afternoon. **Expansion joints** — the metal 'teeth' you bump over — let the deck move.
- **Earthquakes** — shake the ground beneath the supports.
- **Water** — river currents, floods, debris and **scour** (water digging away soil around foundations).

**Checking the temperature number:** steel expands by roughly 12 millionths of its length per °C. For a 1,000 m deck and a 35 °C swing: 1,000 × 0.000012 × 35 = 0.42 m. ✓

**Safety factors.** Engineers design for loads larger than expected and materials weaker than tested, so that uncertainty never leads to failure.
keyTerms: Dead load — the structure's own weight
Live load — moving loads like traffic
Expansion joint — a gap that lets the deck lengthen and shorten
Scour — erosion of soil around foundations by flowing water

check.q: Why do bridges have expansion joints?
options: To let the deck expand and contract with temperature
check.why: Materials change length with temperature, and joints allow this movement without cracking the structure.

sections.h: Tension, compression, bending and shear
sections.md:
Every part of a bridge is being **pushed**, **pulled**, or both.

- **Compression** squeezes a member shorter. Stone, brick and concrete are very strong in compression. Too much compression on a slender member causes **buckling** — it bows sideways and collapses, like a plastic ruler pressed from both ends.
- **Tension** stretches a member longer. Steel cables and rods are excellent in tension; stone and plain concrete are weak and crack.

**Bending.** Lay a plank across two bricks and stand in the middle. It sags. The **top surface is squeezed** (compression) and the **bottom surface is stretched** (tension). Somewhere in between is the **neutral axis**, with neither. This is why beams are often shaped like an **I**: most material is placed at the top and bottom flanges, where the stresses are largest, with a thin web in between — strong and light.

**Shear.** Forces that try to slide one part of the material past another — like scissors. Shear is highest near supports in a beam.

**Stress** is force per unit area: stress = force ÷ area, measured in pascals (N/m²), usually megapascals (MPa). A steel rod of cross-section 0.001 m² carrying 200,000 N has a stress of 200,000 ÷ 0.001 = 200,000,000 Pa = **200 MPa** — within the capacity of typical structural steel, which yields at around 250–350 MPa or more depending on grade.

**Try it:** press a sponge from above with a line drawn on its side — the top lines crowd together, the bottom lines spread apart.

check.q: When a beam sags under a load at its middle, its bottom surface is in:
check.why: Sagging lengthens the bottom fibres, putting them in tension, while the top is compressed.

sections.h: Materials: stone, steel and concrete
sections.md:
**Stone and brick** — superb in compression, weak in tension. That's why ancient bridges are arches, which keep everything squeezed. Some Roman stone arch bridges still stand after nearly two thousand years.

**Iron and steel** — strong in both tension and compression. Wrought iron and then steel enabled the great truss and suspension bridges of the 19th and 20th centuries. Steel's weaknesses: it **rusts** (it needs paint, galvanising or weathering steel), and it loses strength at very high temperatures.

**Concrete** — a mix of cement, sand, gravel and water. Strong in compression, cheap, mouldable, but weak in tension (roughly a tenth of its compressive strength).

**Reinforced concrete (RCC)** — embed steel bars (rebar) where tension occurs, usually near the bottom of beams. Concrete handles compression; steel handles tension. The two expand at nearly the same rate with temperature, so they work well together. Most Indian flyovers are reinforced or prestressed concrete.

**Prestressed concrete** — steel tendons are tensioned (stretched) and anchored, squeezing the concrete *before* any load arrives. When traffic later tries to stretch the bottom of the beam, it first has to undo this built-in compression. The result: longer spans, slimmer beams, fewer cracks. Many metro viaducts are built from prestressed concrete segments.

**Modern additions** — high-performance concrete, corrosion-resistant steels, and fibre-reinforced polymers for strengthening old bridges.

| Material | Compression | Tension | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stone/brick | Excellent | Poor | Arches |
| Steel | Excellent | Excellent | Trusses, cables, arches |
| Plain concrete | Good | Poor | Foundations, piers |
| Reinforced concrete | Good | Good (via steel) | Beams, decks, flyovers |
| Prestressed concrete | Good | Very good | Long concrete spans, viaducts |

check.q: Why is steel placed near the bottom of a reinforced concrete beam?
options: Because that's where tension occurs and concrete is weak in tension
check.why: In a sagging beam the bottom is in tension, so steel bars there carry the pull that concrete cannot.

sections.h: Beam bridges and trusses
sections.md:
**The beam bridge** is the simplest: a horizontal beam resting on supports at each end (abutments) and perhaps on piers in between. Every flyover and most river bridges in India use beams. Their limit: as the span gets longer, bending grows rapidly. For a uniformly loaded simple beam, the maximum bending moment grows with the **square of the span** — double the span and bending roughly quadruples. So simple beams become heavy and uneconomic beyond a few tens of metres, unless made deep, boxed or continuous over several supports.

**Box girders** — hollow rectangular or trapezoidal sections — are strong against both bending and twisting, and are widely used in modern viaducts.

**The truss** replaces a solid beam with a lattice of straight members joined in **triangles**. Why triangles? A square frame with hinged corners can be pushed into a rhombus; a triangle cannot change shape without changing the length of a side. So a truss is rigid yet light.

In a simple truss bridge under load, the **top chord** is in compression, the **bottom chord** in tension, and the diagonals alternate between tension and compression depending on their direction. Common patterns are named after their inventors: **Pratt**, **Howe** and **Warren** trusses.

India's railway network is full of steel truss bridges, many from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Kolkata's **Howrah Bridge** (opened 1943) is a giant cantilever truss — two arms reaching out from tall towers and meeting in a suspended central span, with no piers in the busy Hooghly river below. Its main span is about 457 metres.

fig.alt: A Warren truss with red top chord, green bottom chord and a yellow block moving across.

check.q: Why are trusses made of triangles?
options: A triangle can't change shape without changing a side's length, so it's rigid
check.why: Triangles are inherently rigid, letting light members form a stiff structure.

sections.h: The arch: turning weight into a squeeze
sections.md:
An arch carries load by **compression**. Weight on top pushes down and outward along the curve; each stone (voussoir) presses on its neighbours, and the push flows around the curve to the supports. The keystone at the top locks the arch once complete. During construction, a temporary wooden frame called **centering** holds the stones until the keystone is placed.

**Thrust.** An arch doesn't just push down; it pushes **outward** at its feet. That outward thrust must be resisted by solid **abutments** — rock walls of a gorge are ideal — or by a tie (a 'tied arch', where a tension member connects the two feet like a bowstring).

**Shape matters.** For a uniform load, the ideal arch follows a curve close to a parabola; a hanging chain forms a **catenary**, and flipping that shape upside down gives an arch in pure compression under its own weight — a trick architects have used for centuries.

**Steel and concrete arches** extend the idea to huge spans. The **Chenab Rail Bridge** in Jammu and Kashmir uses a steel arch with a span of about 467 metres, springing from the rock on either side of the gorge, carrying the deck on steel columns. Its designers had to consider very high winds, earthquakes and even blast resistance; the arch members are steel boxes filled with concrete in places for added stiffness.

> **Did you know?** The Chenab bridge's height above the river — about 359 m — makes it widely described as the world's highest railway arch bridge.

fig.alt: A steel arch drawing itself across a gorge with dots flowing down each side into the rock.

check.q: Besides pushing down, the feet of an arch push:
check.why: Arches produce horizontal thrust at their supports, which strong abutments or a tie must resist.

sections.h: Suspension and cable-stayed bridges
sections.md:
For the longest spans, engineers turn to **tension**, using steel cables that are extraordinarily strong for their weight.

**Suspension bridges.** Two main cables drape over tall towers and are anchored into massive **anchorages** at each end. Vertical **hangers** drop from the main cables to hold the deck. The deck's weight pulls the cables into tension; the cables push down on the towers (compression) and pull on the anchorages. Suspension bridges hold the record spans — over 2 kilometres between towers for the longest. Kolkata's second Hooghly bridge isn't a suspension bridge; India's well-known suspension bridges include the Lakshman Jhula footbridge at Rishikesh (a historic pedestrian bridge).

**Cable-stayed bridges.** Cables run directly from the towers to the deck in straight lines, in a fan or harp pattern. No anchorages are needed, because the horizontal pulls of cables on either side of a tower balance each other and are carried as compression in the deck. They're very efficient for spans of roughly 200 to 1,000 metres and have become common worldwide. Indian examples include **Vidyasagar Setu** in Kolkata (opened 1992, main span about 457 m), the **Bandra–Worli Sea Link** in Mumbai (opened 2009), and the **Signature Bridge** in Delhi (opened 2018).

**The danger of wind.** In 1940, the Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge in the USA twisted itself apart in a moderate wind, just four months after opening. Its deck was slender and shaped in a way that let wind feed energy into twisting oscillations (an aerodynamic effect called flutter). Since then, long-span bridges are tested in **wind tunnels**, and decks are shaped like aerofoils or stiffened with trusses.

right.title: Cable-stayed
points: Straight cables from towers to deck
e.g. Vidyasagar Setu, Bandra–Worli Sea Link

check.q: Why don't cable-stayed bridges need large anchorages?
options: Cable pulls on both sides of each tower balance, and the deck carries the horizontal force
check.why: Balanced cable forces on each side of a tower and compression in the deck remove the need for ground anchorages.

sections.h: Foundations, earthquakes and fatigue
sections.md:
**Foundations.** All forces end up in the ground. On firm rock, a bridge can sit on shallow footings. On soft river silt — common on the Ganga and Brahmaputra plains — engineers use deep **piles** (long columns driven or bored into the ground) or **well foundations** (large hollow caissons sunk deep below the riverbed), a technique long used on Indian rivers. Foundations must go below the deepest expected **scour** during floods.

**Earthquakes.** Ground shaking can make bridge decks slide off their supports or crack piers. Designers use:
- **Bearings** that allow controlled movement, and **seismic isolation** bearings that reduce the shaking passed to the deck.
- **Restrainers** that stop spans falling off supports.
- **Ductile** design: steel reinforcement detailed so piers bend and deform without sudden collapse.

**Fatigue.** Every passing truck or train flexes the bridge slightly. Millions of cycles can grow tiny cracks in steel, especially at welds and joints — this is **fatigue**. Engineers limit stress ranges at vulnerable details and inspect regularly.

**Corrosion and ageing.** Salt from sea air, water leaking through joints and carbon dioxide gradually corrode steel inside concrete. Protective coatings, good drainage, adequate concrete cover over rebar and regular maintenance extend life.

**Inspection and monitoring.** Bridges are inspected visually and with tools: ultrasonic testing for cracks in steel, cover meters for rebar, and on major bridges, **sensors** that continuously measure strain, vibration, temperature and wind. When warning signs appear, engineers can restrict loads, repair or strengthen.

check.q: Why must river bridge foundations go below the expected scour depth?
options: Because floods can wash away soil around shallow foundations, undermining them
check.why: Scour during floods removes soil around foundations; if they aren't deep enough, the bridge can lose support.

sections.h: Indian bridges and the people who build them
sections.md:
India has an extraordinary range of bridges:

- **Living root bridges, Meghalaya** — Khasi and Jaintia communities guide the roots of rubber fig trees across streams over many years, creating bridges that grow stronger with age.
- **Howrah Bridge, Kolkata (1943)** — steel cantilever truss over the Hooghly; one of the busiest bridges in the world.
- **Pamban Bridge, Tamil Nadu (1914)** — India's first sea bridge, linking Rameswaram island, with a lifting span for ships; a new vertical-lift rail bridge was built alongside it in the 2020s.
- **Vidyasagar Setu, Kolkata (1992)** — cable-stayed road bridge.
- **Bandra–Worli Sea Link, Mumbai (2009)** — cable-stayed over the sea.
- **Bogibeel Bridge, Assam (2018)** — India's longest rail-cum-road bridge, about 4.9 km across the Brahmaputra.
- **Chenab Rail Bridge, J&K** — the steel arch high above the Chenab, opened to trains in 2025.
- **Mumbai Trans Harbour Link (Atal Setu, 2024)** — about 21.8 km, India's longest sea bridge.

Behind every bridge are teams: **structural engineers** who calculate forces; **geotechnical engineers** who study soil and rock; **construction engineers** and skilled workers — welders, crane operators, concrete crews, divers; **surveyors**; and **maintenance teams** who inspect for decades.

**How you could become one:** study physics and mathematics at school; take civil engineering in college; specialise in structures. But anyone can start now — build a bridge from straws or ice-cream sticks and test how much weight it holds. You'll rediscover triangles, arches and tension for yourself.

rd-engineering-cpu.title: How a CPU Runs a Program
rd-engineering-cpu.subtitle: From switches to instructions: fetch, decode, execute — billions of times a second

sections.h: What happens when you tap 'Pay'
sections.md:
You tap *Pay ₹250* in a UPI app. In the fraction of a second before the green tick, the processor in your phone carries out many millions of tiny steps: reading your touch, drawing the screen, encrypting the message, talking to the network. Each step is absurdly simple — add two numbers, compare two numbers, copy a number from one place to another, jump to a different instruction. The magic is that the chip does billions of these simple steps every second, without error, for years.

The **CPU** (central processing unit) is the part of a computer that runs programs. This read follows a program all the way down:

1. Bits and transistors — the switches underneath.
2. Logic gates — building decisions from switches.
3. Binary numbers and the adder.
4. Registers, memory and the instruction set.
5. The fetch–decode–execute cycle, step by step.
6. The clock and why GHz isn't everything.
7. Making it fast: pipelines, caches and multiple cores.
8. From your code to machine instructions.

check.q: Each individual step a CPU performs is:
options: Very simple, like adding or comparing numbers
check.why: CPUs build all behaviour from huge numbers of very simple operations executed extremely quickly.

sections.h: Bits and transistors: the switches underneath
sections.md:
Everything inside a computer is represented by **bits** — values that are either **0** or **1**. Physically, a bit is a voltage: low (near 0 volts) means 0, high (around 1 volt in modern chips) means 1.

The device that controls these voltages is the **transistor**, an electrically controlled switch. The kind used in processors is the **MOSFET**. It has three terminals: **source**, **drain** and **gate**. Apply a voltage to the gate and current can flow between source and drain (switch ON); remove it and the path closes (switch OFF). No moving parts — just electric fields in silicon.

Two kinds of MOSFET, **n-type** and **p-type**, are paired in a design called **CMOS** (complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor). In CMOS, one transistor of the pair is always off when the other is on, so very little current flows except when switching — which is why chips can hold billions of transistors without melting.

**How small?** Modern processors contain billions of transistors; leading-edge phone and laptop chips pack in tens of billions. Feature sizes are measured in nanometres (a nanometre is a billionth of a metre — a human hair is roughly 80,000–100,000 nm wide). The 'nm' names manufacturers use for process generations (like '3 nm') are now marketing labels rather than a single physical measurement.

> **Did you know?** The first transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in 1947. The first commercial single-chip microprocessor, Intel's 4004 (1971), had about 2,300 transistors.

sections.h: Logic gates: decisions from switches
sections.md:
Wire transistors together and you get **logic gates**, circuits whose output depends on their inputs according to simple rules.

| Gate | Output is 1 when… |
|---|---|
| **NOT** | the input is 0 (it flips the bit) |
| **AND** | both inputs are 1 |
| **OR** | at least one input is 1 |
| **XOR** | exactly one input is 1 |
| **NAND** | NOT AND — output 0 only when both inputs are 1 |

**Truth table for AND and XOR:**

| A | B | A AND B | A XOR B |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

A CMOS NOT gate (inverter) needs just two transistors; a NAND gate needs four. Remarkably, **NAND alone is universal**: any logic circuit can be built from NAND gates only.

Gates are combined into larger blocks:
- **Multiplexers** choose one of several inputs.
- **Decoders** turn a binary code into a single active line.
- **Flip-flops** — gates wired in a loop — **remember** one bit. This is the basis of registers and fast memory.

Everything a CPU does — arithmetic, comparisons, choosing which instruction to run next — is built from these gates.
keyTerms: Logic gate — a circuit computing a simple rule on bits
Truth table — a table listing outputs for all input combinations
Flip-flop — a circuit that stores one bit

check.q: What is the output of XOR when both inputs are 1?
check.why: XOR outputs 1 only when exactly one input is 1; with both 1, it outputs 0.

sections.h: Binary numbers and the adder
sections.md:
Computers represent numbers in **binary** (base 2). Each position is a power of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128…

- 1011 in binary = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = **11** in decimal.
- 25 in decimal = 16 + 8 + 1 = **11001** in binary.

Eight bits make a **byte**, which can hold 2⁸ = 256 different values (0–255). Modern CPUs work with 64-bit numbers.

**Adding in binary** follows the same carrying rules as decimal: 0+0 = 0; 0+1 = 1; 1+1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1); 1+1+1 = 11 (write 1, carry 1).

**Example:** 0110 (6) + 0111 (7)
- Rightmost: 0 + 1 = 1, carry 0.
- Next: 1 + 1 = 10 → write 0, carry 1.
- Next: 1 + 1 + carry 1 = 11 → write 1, carry 1.
- Next: 0 + 0 + carry 1 = 1.
- Result: **1101** = 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = **13** ✓ (6 + 7 = 13).

**The half adder.** Look at adding two single bits: the **sum** bit is A XOR B, and the **carry** bit is A AND B. Just two gates!

**The full adder** also takes a carry-in, and is built from two half adders and an OR gate. Chain 64 full adders, each passing its carry to the next, and you can add 64-bit numbers. (Real CPUs use faster 'carry-lookahead' designs so they don't wait for the carry to ripple through all 64.)

Subtraction uses a trick called **two's complement**, which lets the same adder subtract. The **ALU** (arithmetic logic unit) combines adders and logic circuits to perform add, subtract, AND, OR, compare and shift.

sections.h: Registers, memory and the instruction set
sections.md:
**Registers** are a small number of very fast storage slots inside the CPU — typically a few dozen, each holding one 64-bit value. Calculations happen on registers.

**Main memory (RAM)** holds programs and data — billions of bytes, each with a numbered **address**. It's far larger than the registers but much slower to reach.

**Special registers:**
- **Program counter (PC)** — the address of the next instruction to run.
- **Instruction register** — holds the instruction currently being worked on.
- **Flags / status register** — records results like *zero*, *negative* or *overflow* from the last operation, used for decisions.
- **Stack pointer** — tracks a region of memory used for function calls.

**The instruction set architecture (ISA)** is the vocabulary of instructions a CPU understands. Common families: **x86-64** (most desktop and laptop PCs), **ARM** (almost all phones, and increasingly laptops and servers) and **RISC-V** (an open standard growing in use, including in Indian research such as the Shakti processor project at IIT Madras).

Instructions fall into a few types:

| Type | Example (simplified) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Load | LOAD R1, [1000] | Copy the value at memory address 1000 into register R1 |
| Store | STORE R1, [1004] | Copy R1 into memory address 1004 |
| Arithmetic | ADD R3, R1, R2 | R3 = R1 + R2 |
| Compare | CMP R1, R2 | Set flags based on R1 − R2 |
| Branch | JUMP-IF-ZERO 40 | If the zero flag is set, continue at instruction 40 |

Each instruction is itself stored in memory as a binary number — the **machine code**. Some bits say *what* operation; others say *which registers* or *what address*.

> **Did you know?** Storing instructions in the same memory as data — the 'stored-program' idea — is associated with the 1940s work of John von Neumann and others. It's why the same computer can run a game, then a spreadsheet: just load different instructions.

check.q: What does the program counter hold?
options: The result of the last addition
The address of the next instruction
check.why: The program counter points to where the next instruction is in memory.

sections.h: The fetch–decode–execute cycle
sections.md:
Here is the heart of every CPU. Over and over, it does:

1. **Fetch** — read the instruction at the address in the program counter from memory into the instruction register. Increase the PC to point to the next instruction.
2. **Decode** — the control unit examines the instruction's bits and works out what to do: which operation, which registers, which memory address.
3. **Execute** — the ALU performs the operation, or memory is read or written, or the PC is changed for a branch.
4. **Write back** — store the result in a register (or memory).

Then repeat.

**Let's trace a tiny program** that adds 5 and 7 and stores the answer. Memory address 1000 holds 5; 1004 holds 7.

| PC | Instruction | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | LOAD R1, [1000] | R1 = 5 |
| 1 | LOAD R2, [1004] | R2 = 7 |
| 2 | ADD R3, R1, R2 | R3 = 12 |
| 3 | STORE R3, [1008] | memory[1008] = 12 |
| 4 | HALT | stop |

Each row is one full fetch–decode–execute cycle. After row 2, R3 holds 5 + 7 = 12. ✓

**Decisions and loops** come from compare and branch. To count down from 3 to 0:

| PC | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 0 | SET R1, 3 |
| 1 | SUB R1, R1, 1 |
| 2 | JUMP-IF-NOT-ZERO 1 |
| 3 | HALT |

R1 goes 3 → 2 (jump back) → 1 (jump back) → 0 (zero flag set, no jump) → HALT. Every `if`, `while` and `for` you write in a programming language ends up as compare-and-branch.

check.why: During decode, the control unit interprets the instruction's bits to set up the right operation.

sections.h: The clock, and why GHz isn't everything
sections.md:
A CPU's steps are synchronised by a **clock** — an electrical signal ticking at a steady rate. A 3 GHz clock ticks 3 billion times per second, so each tick lasts 1 ÷ 3,000,000,000 s ≈ **0.33 nanoseconds**. In that time, light travels only about 10 centimetres.

On each tick, flip-flops capture new values and the logic between them has one tick to settle. The clock speed is limited by how fast the slowest path of gates can switch, and by heat: power use rises steeply with frequency and voltage. That's why clock speeds largely stopped climbing in the mid-2000s, at a few gigahertz.

**Performance isn't just GHz.** A useful way to think:

> Time for a program = number of instructions × cycles per instruction ÷ clock rate

A chip at 3 GHz that completes 4 instructions per cycle on average does more work than a 4 GHz chip completing 1. So engineers worked on doing **more per tick** — with pipelines, multiple execution units and better prediction.

**Example.** A program needs 6 billion instructions. Chip A: 3 GHz, 2 instructions per cycle → 6 × 10⁹ ÷ (2 × 3 × 10⁹) = **1 second**. Chip B: 4 GHz, 1 instruction per cycle → 6 × 10⁹ ÷ (1 × 4 × 10⁹) = **1.5 seconds**. The slower clock wins.

**Heat and power.** Phone chips are designed for efficiency; they speed up briefly for heavy tasks and slow down to save battery and avoid overheating ('thermal throttling').

sections.h: Making it fast: pipelines, caches and cores
sections.md:
**Pipelining.** Imagine a dosa counter with four people: one pours batter, one spreads it, one adds filling, one folds and serves. Each dosa still takes four steps, but a new dosa finishes every step-time because all four workers are busy on different dosas. A CPU **pipeline** does the same: while one instruction executes, the next is decoding, and the one after is being fetched. Modern CPUs have pipelines of 10–20 stages.

**Hazards.** Pipelines stall when an instruction needs a result that isn't ready yet, or when a **branch** means the CPU doesn't know which instruction comes next. **Branch prediction** guesses — often correctly over 90% of the time in typical code — and if wrong, the CPU throws away the work and restarts. **Out-of-order execution** lets the CPU run later independent instructions while waiting for earlier slow ones. **Superscalar** designs have several ALUs so multiple instructions execute per cycle.

**Caches.** Fetching from main memory can take on the order of 100 nanoseconds — hundreds of clock cycles. So CPUs keep copies of recently used data in small, fast **caches**:

| Level | Typical size | Approximate speed |
|---|---|---|
| Registers | ~a few hundred bytes | 1 cycle |
| L1 cache | tens of KB per core | a few cycles |
| L2 cache | hundreds of KB–few MB | ~10+ cycles |
| L3 cache | several to tens of MB (shared) | tens of cycles |
| RAM | GBs | hundreds of cycles |
| SSD storage | hundreds of GB–TB | far slower still |

Caches work because programs tend to reuse recent data (**temporal locality**) and access nearby data (**spatial locality**).

**Multiple cores.** Since clock speeds stalled, chips put several complete CPUs — **cores** — on one chip. A phone might have 8 cores: some high-performance, some power-saving. Programs must be written to split work into parallel threads to benefit. **GPUs** take this further with thousands of simpler cores, ideal for graphics and AI.

check.q: Why do CPUs have caches?
options: Because main memory is much slower than the CPU, so recently used data is kept close
check.why: Caches hide memory delays by keeping frequently used data in small, fast storage near the cores.

sections.h: From your code to machine instructions
sections.md:
Nobody writes machine code by hand any more (well, almost nobody). Here's how a line of code becomes something the CPU can run.

Suppose you write, in a language like C:

> total = price + tax;

1. **The compiler** translates it into instructions for the target ISA — something like: load *price* into R1, load *tax* into R2, ADD R3, R1, R2, store R3 into *total*.
2. **The assembler and linker** turn these into binary machine code and combine them with libraries into an executable file.
3. **The operating system** (Android, Windows, Linux, iOS) loads the program into memory, sets the program counter to its first instruction, and lets it run — while switching between many programs hundreds of times a second so they appear to run simultaneously.

Languages like **Python** and **JavaScript** are often run by an **interpreter** or a **just-in-time (JIT) compiler** — itself a program that reads your code and executes matching machine instructions, sometimes compiling hot sections on the fly for speed.

**Layers of abstraction:**

| Layer | Example |
|---|---|
| Application | UPI app |
| High-level language | Kotlin, Swift, Python |
| Operating system | Android, iOS |
| Instruction set | ARM |
| Microarchitecture | Pipelines, caches |
| Logic gates | AND, XOR, flip-flops |
| Transistors | CMOS switches |
| Physics | Electrons in silicon |

Each layer hides the complexity below it. A programmer writing a payments app doesn't think about transistors — but every tap of *Pay* still turns into transistors switching billions of times.

> **Did you know?** India is building semiconductor manufacturing and design capacity under the India Semiconductor Mission, launched in 2021, alongside long-standing chip-design work by engineers in cities like Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

check.q: What does a compiler do?
options: Translates high-level code into machine instructions
check.why: The compiler converts human-readable code into the binary instructions a specific CPU understands.

summary: A CPU runs programs by performing billions of very simple operations per second.
Bits are 0 or 1, represented as low or high voltage.
Transistors (MOSFETs) are voltage-controlled switches; CMOS pairs them to save power.
Logic gates (NOT, AND, OR, XOR, NAND) combine bits; NAND alone is universal.
Flip-flops store bits and form registers.
Binary uses powers of two; a byte has 256 values.
A half adder: sum = XOR, carry = AND; chained full adders add large numbers.
Registers are tiny and fast; RAM is large and slower; the PC points to the next instruction.
The ISA (x86-64, ARM, RISC-V) defines load, store, arithmetic, compare and branch instructions.
The cycle: fetch, decode, execute, write back — loops and ifs are compare-and-branch.
Clock rate sets ticks per second, but work per tick matters as much.
Pipelines, branch prediction, out-of-order and superscalar execution do more per tick.
Caches hide slow memory using temporal and spatial locality; multiple cores add parallelism.
Compilers, interpreters and operating systems turn your code into running machine instructions.

rd-engineering-engines-ev-motors.title: How Engines and EV Motors Work
rd-engineering-engines-ev-motors.subtitle: Controlled explosions versus silent magnets — the two machines racing to move India

sections.h: Two scooters at a traffic light
sections.md:
The signal turns green at a crossing in Bengaluru. A petrol scooter coughs, revs and buzzes away. Beside it, an electric scooter simply *glides* off — almost silent, and somehow quicker off the line.

Both turn stored energy into motion. But they do it in utterly different ways:

- The petrol engine burns fuel in tiny, controlled **explosions** thousands of times a minute, pushing pistons that turn a crankshaft.
- The electric motor uses **magnetic forces** between currents and magnets to spin a rotor directly, drawing energy from a battery.

In this read you will learn:

1. What *work, power and torque* mean.
2. How a four-stroke petrol engine works, stroke by stroke.
3. Diesel engines and why they are different.
4. The thermodynamic limit on any heat engine.
5. How gears and transmissions match an engine to the road.
6. How an electric motor makes force from magnetism.
7. How EV motors, inverters and batteries work together, and how charging works.
8. Comparing the two honestly — efficiency, emissions, cost — and the hybrids in between.

sections.h: Work, power and torque
sections.md:
**Work** is done when a force moves something: W = F × d, measured in joules. Pushing a 100 kg scooter with a 200 N force for 10 m does 2,000 J of work.

**Power** is how fast work is done: P = W ÷ t, measured in watts. A scooter motor rated 4 kW can deliver 4,000 joules every second. (Older units: 1 horsepower ≈ 746 W.)

**Torque** is a *turning* force: torque = force × perpendicular distance from the axis, measured in newton-metres (N·m). A spanner 0.3 m long, pushed with 50 N, gives 15 N·m of torque on a nut.

For anything spinning, **power = torque × angular speed**:

**P = τ × ω**, where ω (radians per second) = 2π × revolutions per second.

This single equation explains a lot. A truck engine needs huge torque at low speed to start a heavy load; a racing bike engine makes moderate torque but at very high rpm, giving high power. Electric motors give **maximum torque from zero speed**, which is why EVs leap off the line.

> **Did you know?** Car brochures quote both power (kW or bhp) and torque (N·m). Torque tells you how strongly it pulls; power tells you how fast it can keep doing so.
keyTerms: Work — force × distance (joules)
Power — rate of doing work (watts)
Torque — turning effect of a force (N·m)

check.q: An engine produces 100 N·m at 3,000 rpm. What is its power, approximately?

sections.h: The four-stroke petrol engine
sections.md:
Most petrol engines in bikes and cars follow the **four-stroke (Otto) cycle**, first built by Nikolaus Otto in 1876. A **piston** slides in a **cylinder**; a **connecting rod** links it to a **crankshaft**, which turns up-and-down motion into rotation. **Valves** at the top open and close in time, driven by a **camshaft**.

1. **Intake.** The intake valve opens; the piston moves down, drawing in a mixture of air and fine petrol spray (from a fuel injector).
2. **Compression.** Both valves close; the piston moves up, squeezing the mixture to around one-tenth of its volume (a **compression ratio** of about 10:1). The gas heats up.
3. **Power.** Just before the top, the **spark plug** fires. The mixture burns in a few milliseconds; temperature leaps above 2,000 °C and pressure soars, shoving the piston down. This is the only stroke that produces work.
4. **Exhaust.** The exhaust valve opens; the piston rises and pushes the burnt gases out to the silencer.

Four strokes take **two turns** of the crankshaft. At 6,000 rpm, each cylinder fires 3,000 times a minute — 50 times a second. A heavy **flywheel** and multiple cylinders smooth out the jerky power pulses.

Modern engines add electronic fuel injection, sensors that monitor oxygen in the exhaust, and **catalytic converters** that convert carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides into less harmful gases. India's **Bharat Stage VI** norms (from April 2020) made these systems far stricter.

check.why: Each stroke is half a rotation, so four strokes need two full turns of the crankshaft.

sections.h: Keeping an engine alive: cooling, lubrication, starting
sections.md:
An engine is not just a piston. Several support systems keep it working for hundreds of thousands of kilometres.

**Cooling.** Combustion gas is hotter than the melting point of aluminium. Engines survive because the flame touches metal only for milliseconds and the walls are constantly cooled. Small bikes use **air cooling** — the fins on a motorcycle cylinder give a large surface area for the wind to carry heat away. Cars use **liquid cooling**: a pump pushes coolant (water plus glycol, which raises the boiling point and stops corrosion) through passages in the block to the **radiator** at the front, where a fan blows air through thin fins. A **thermostat** valve keeps the engine near about 90 °C — warm enough to run efficiently, cool enough to be safe.

**Lubrication.** Metal sliding on metal would weld itself together. An oil pump forces engine oil into bearings and onto cylinder walls, forming a film only micrometres thick that keeps surfaces apart. Oil also carries away heat and dirt — which is why it darkens and must be changed.

**Starting.** An engine cannot start itself: something must turn it until the first power strokes happen. Older scooters used a **kick-starter**; today an electric **starter motor**, powered by a 12 V lead-acid battery, spins the crankshaft. Once running, an **alternator** driven by a belt recharges the battery and runs the lights.

**Fuel and air.** Old engines used a **carburettor**, which sucked petrol into the air stream through a narrow throat (the Venturi effect). Modern engines use **fuel injection**: an electronic control unit (ECU) reads sensors for air flow, temperature, throttle position and exhaust oxygen, and opens injectors for exactly the right few milliseconds. The ideal petrol–air ratio by mass is about **14.7 : 1**.

> **Did you know?** Many new Indian cars switch the engine off at traffic lights and restart it instantly when you press the clutch — 'start-stop' systems save fuel that idling would waste.

check.q: What is the main job of the radiator's thermostat?
options: To cool the engine as much as possible
To keep the engine near its best operating temperature
check.why: The thermostat lets coolant reach the radiator only as needed, holding the engine near about 90 °C where it runs efficiently and safely.

sections.h: Diesel: fire by squeezing
sections.md:
Rudolf Diesel patented his engine in the 1890s. It uses the same four strokes, but with a crucial difference: **no spark plug**.

- On intake, the cylinder takes in **only air**.
- On compression, the air is squeezed far harder — compression ratios of about **15:1 to 22:1**. Rapid compression heats air strongly (just as a bicycle pump gets warm), to around 500–700 °C.
- At the top, diesel is injected at very high pressure (common-rail systems reach 1,500–2,500 bar). It **ignites on its own** in the hot air.

Higher compression means higher efficiency and more torque at low speed, which is why diesel powers trucks, buses, tractors, ships, generator sets and many Indian Railways locomotives. Diesel engines, however, produce more nitrogen oxides and soot; BS-VI diesels need particulate filters and urea-based selective catalytic reduction (the AdBlue / DEF tank in trucks).

**Two-stroke engines**, once common in Indian scooters and autorickshaws, combine strokes so each down-stroke is a power stroke. They are light and simple but burn some lubricating oil and let fuel escape unburnt, causing smoke. Emission rules largely phased them out of road vehicles.

| | Petrol (spark ignition) | Diesel (compression ignition) |
|---|---|---|
| Ignition | spark plug | heat of compressed air |
| Compression ratio | about 9–13 : 1 | about 15–22 : 1 |
| Typical peak efficiency | 30–38% | 40–45% (large engines over 50%) |
| Strength | smooth, high rpm | high torque at low rpm |
| Main pollutants to control | CO, HC, NOx | NOx, soot |

**Turbochargers** use the hot exhaust to spin a turbine, which drives a compressor that forces extra air into the cylinders. More air allows more fuel to be burnt, so a small engine gives big-engine power — common in modern diesel and petrol cars.

check.q: How is fuel ignited in a diesel engine?
options: By the high temperature of strongly compressed air
check.why: Diesel engines compress air so much that it becomes hot enough to ignite injected fuel without a spark.

sections.h: The heat-engine limit: why most fuel energy becomes heat
sections.md:
Petrol carries about 34 MJ per litre, yet a typical car engine turns only around **a quarter to a third** of that into motion at the wheels on average. Where does the rest go? Out of the exhaust and radiator as heat.

This is not just poor design. It is a law of physics. Any **heat engine** takes heat from a hot source, turns some into work, and must dump the rest to a cold sink. The **second law of thermodynamics** sets the best possible efficiency, found by Sadi Carnot in 1824:

**η_max = 1 − T_cold ÷ T_hot** (temperatures in kelvin)

With a hot gas at about 2,000 K and surroundings at 300 K, η_max = 1 − 300/2,000 = **85%**. But real engines fall far short: the gas is hot only briefly, heat leaks through cylinder walls, friction steals some, pumping air in and out costs some, and the engine often runs at part load in traffic, where efficiency is worst.

For an **ideal Otto cycle**, efficiency depends on compression ratio r: η = 1 − 1 ÷ r^(γ−1), where γ ≈ 1.4 for air. With r = 10, r^0.4 ≈ 2.51, so η ≈ 1 − 0.40 = **60%** in theory. Real engines get about half that. Raising compression helps, but too high and petrol **knocks** — ignites too early — which is why fuel octane ratings matter.

check.q: According to Carnot, what limits the efficiency of any heat engine?
options: The temperatures of its hot source and cold sink
check.why: The second law means efficiency can never exceed 1 − T_cold/T_hot, so some heat must always be rejected.

sections.h: Gears and transmissions: matching engine to road
sections.md:
A petrol engine only makes useful power between roughly 1,000 and 7,000 rpm, and it cannot run at zero rpm at all. Yet a car's wheels must turn from standstill up to about 1,500 rpm at highway speed. The **gearbox** bridges this gap.

Gears trade speed for torque. If a small gear with 15 teeth drives a large gear with 45 teeth, the big gear turns **three times slower** but with **three times the torque** (ignoring small friction losses). Power — torque × speed — stays about the same. First gear in a car might have a ratio near 3.5 : 1 for climbing a ghat road from rest; fifth gear might be near 0.8 : 1 for cruising on an expressway at low rpm.

**The clutch** lets the driver disconnect the spinning engine from the gearbox while changing gears or stopping, using friction plates pressed together by springs. Automatic transmissions do this with a fluid coupling (torque converter), with a **CVT** (a belt running on cone-shaped pulleys that changes ratio smoothly — used in gearless scooters), or with robotic clutches (AMT, popular in Indian hatchbacks).

After the gearbox, a **differential** splits the drive between left and right wheels and lets the outer wheel spin faster on a turn — otherwise tyres would scrub and skid around every corner.

Electric motors, by contrast, work efficiently from 0 to well over 10,000 rpm, so most EVs need just **one fixed reduction gear**. That is why an EV has no gear lever and no clutch.

> **Did you know?** A bicycle with gears follows exactly the same rule: a big rear sprocket gives more torque for hills, a small one more speed on the flat.

check.why: The ratio is 60/20 = 3, so torque is multiplied by 3: 50 × 3 = 150 N·m, while speed drops to one-third.

sections.h: The electric motor: force from magnetism
sections.md:
In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a current-carrying wire deflects a compass. Soon Michael Faraday built the first device that turned electricity into continuous motion (1821). The principle is simple:

**A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force.** F = B × I × L, where B is magnetic field strength (tesla), I is current and L is the length of wire in the field. Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction.

Put a loop of wire between magnets: one side is pushed up, the other down — a torque. The loop turns. To keep it turning the same way, the current must reverse every half-turn. In the classic **DC motor**, a **commutator** (split copper ring) and **brushes** do this switching mechanically.

The motors in modern EVs drop the brushes. Instead, the **stator** carries three sets of coils fed with three-phase AC, which creates a **rotating magnetic field**. The rotor follows it:

- **Permanent magnet synchronous motor (PMSM / BLDC):** the rotor contains strong neodymium magnets and spins exactly in step with the rotating field. Highly efficient and compact; used in most Indian e-scooters and many e-cars. Many e-scooters put a BLDC motor right inside the rear wheel — a **hub motor**.
- **Induction motor:** the rotor has copper or aluminium bars; the rotating field *induces* currents in them, which then feel a force. No magnets needed; rugged and cheap; used in ceiling fans, water pumps, industry and some EVs.

A good EV motor converts electrical energy to mechanical energy with **90–97%** efficiency — versus 20–40% for a combustion engine. It has one main moving part, needs no oil changes, and produces full torque from standstill.

options: A rotating magnetic field created by switching current through stator coils in sequence

sections.h: The EV system: battery, inverter, motor, brain
sections.md:
An electric vehicle is a team:

**1. Battery pack.** Hundreds or thousands of **lithium-ion cells**. In each cell, lithium ions shuttle between a graphite anode and a metal-oxide or iron-phosphate cathode through an electrolyte, while electrons go round the outside circuit — through your motor. Indian e-scooters carry about 2–5 kWh; small cars about 25–40 kWh. **LFP** (lithium iron phosphate) chemistry is popular in India for its safety, long life and lack of cobalt.

**2. Battery management system (BMS).** Monitors every cell's voltage and temperature, balances them, and cuts power if anything goes out of the safe range. Heat management matters greatly in Indian summers.

**3. Inverter.** The battery supplies DC; the motor wants three-phase AC of varying frequency. The inverter uses power transistors (IGBTs or silicon-carbide MOSFETs) switching thousands of times a second to synthesise AC waves. Changing the frequency changes motor speed; changing the current changes torque.

**4. Controller.** Software reads your throttle and commands the inverter, millisecond by millisecond.

**5. Reduction gear.** EV motors spin fast (often 10,000–15,000 rpm), so a single fixed gear (around 8:1 to 10:1) reduces speed and multiplies torque at the wheels.

**6. Charger.** Slow AC charging uses the onboard charger; DC fast chargers bypass it and feed the battery directly at tens of kilowatts or more.

**Regenerative braking.** When you lift off the throttle or brake, the motor runs as a **generator** (Faraday's induction), converting the vehicle's kinetic energy back into electricity to recharge the battery. In stop-start city traffic this can recover a meaningful share of energy — and reduces brake wear.

check.q: What does regenerative braking do?
options: Uses the motor as a generator to turn kinetic energy back into stored electrical energy
check.why: Driven by the wheels, the motor generates current that recharges the battery, recovering some braking energy.

sections.h: Charging, range and battery care
sections.md:
Two numbers rule an EV owner's life: **kWh** (how much energy the battery stores) and **Wh/km** (how much the vehicle uses).

**Range ≈ usable battery energy ÷ consumption.** A 3 kWh scooter using 30 Wh/km goes about 3,000 ÷ 30 = 100 km. A 30 kWh car using 150 Wh/km goes about 200 km. Range falls with high speed (air drag grows with the square of speed), heavy loads, hills, very hot or cold weather, and air-conditioning.

**Charging time ≈ energy needed ÷ charger power.** Filling 24 kWh from a 3.3 kW home charger takes about 24 ÷ 3.3 ≈ 7.3 hours — overnight. A 50 kW DC fast charger could add the same energy in roughly half an hour, though charging deliberately slows above about 80% to protect the cells.

**Battery health.** Lithium-ion cells slowly lose capacity with each charge cycle and with heat. Good habits — avoiding leaving the battery at 100% or near 0% for long, parking in shade, and using fast charging when needed rather than always — help it last. Most makers guarantee packs for around 8 years. Battery swapping, popular for e-rickshaws and some scooters in Indian cities, lets a rider exchange an empty pack for a full one in minutes.

**Safety.** A damaged or overheated cell can enter **thermal runaway**, where heat causes reactions that make more heat. This is why the BMS, cell-level fuses, sturdy casing and India's battery testing standards matter, and why owners should use approved chargers.

> **Did you know?** Air drag at 80 km/h is about four times that at 40 km/h — which is why EV range drops noticeably on expressways.

check.q: A 4 kWh scooter uses 25 Wh/km. What is its approximate range?

sections.h: Hybrids and other paths
sections.md:
Between pure petrol and pure electric lies a family of **hybrids**:

- **Mild hybrid:** a small motor-generator helps the engine during acceleration and enables start-stop and limited energy recovery.
- **Strong (full) hybrid:** a bigger battery and motor can drive the car alone at low speeds; the engine and motor share work so the engine mostly runs near its efficient sweet spot. Fuel use in city traffic can drop sharply.
- **Plug-in hybrid:** a larger battery charged from the wall gives a few tens of kilometres of pure electric driving before the engine joins in.

Hybrids attack the engine's biggest weakness — poor efficiency at part load and idling — and recapture braking energy, without needing a charging network.

Other paths matter in India too:

- **CNG** (compressed natural gas) powers lakhs of autorickshaws, taxis and buses; it burns cleaner than diesel with far less soot.
- **Ethanol blending** mixes alcohol made from sugarcane and grain into petrol; India targeted 20% blending (E20) around 2025.
- **Hydrogen fuel cells** combine hydrogen and oxygen to make electricity directly, with only water as exhaust — promising for heavy trucks if green hydrogen becomes cheap.

Each option trades off cost, infrastructure and emissions differently; engineers choose the right tool for each job.

check.q: Why does a strong hybrid save the most fuel in city traffic?
options: The motor handles low-speed driving and braking energy is recovered, so the engine avoids inefficient part-load running
check.why: In stop-start traffic an engine is least efficient; the hybrid's motor covers these phases and regenerative braking recaptures energy.

sections.h: Head to head: an honest comparison
sections.md:
Which is better? Engineers compare on many dimensions:

| | Petrol / diesel vehicle | Battery EV |
|---|---|---|
| Energy conversion on board | about 20–40% | about 85–90% battery-to-wheel |
| Refuelling / charging | minutes at any pump | 30 min to several hours; growing network |
| Range | long, quick to extend | shorter; depends on battery size and heat |
| Running cost per km | higher | usually much lower |
| Maintenance | oil, filters, clutch, many moving parts | few moving parts; battery health matters |
| Tailpipe emissions | CO₂, NOx, particulates in the city | none at the tailpipe |
| Purchase price | lower today | often higher, falling with battery costs |

Two important nuances:

- **Well-to-wheel emissions.** An EV is only as clean as its electricity. When power comes largely from coal, lifetime CO₂ savings are smaller, though studies generally still find EVs comparable or better, and they move pollution away from crowded streets. As India adds solar and wind, EVs get cleaner every year.
- **Battery footprint.** Mining lithium, nickel and cobalt has environmental and social costs. Recycling and new chemistries (LFP, and sodium-ion in development) aim to reduce them.

The likely future is mixed: electric two- and three-wheelers and city buses growing fast; hybrids, CNG and ethanol blends meanwhile; and perhaps hydrogen in some heavy uses. The physics you have learned — Carnot's limit on heat engines, Faraday's induction in motors — explains why the shift is happening.

> **Did you know?** Electric motors already haul most of India's railway traffic: electric locomotives draw 25 kV AC from overhead wires.

check.q: Why is an EV's tailpipe-free operation not the whole story on emissions?
options: Emissions depend on how the electricity is generated and how batteries are made
check.why: Well-to-wheel analysis counts power-plant emissions and battery manufacturing, not just what leaves the vehicle.

workedExamples.q: An EV motor delivers 150 N·m at 6,000 rpm. Find its power.
Find the ideal Otto-cycle efficiency for a compression ratio of 8 (γ = 1.4).
workedExamples.answer: About 56.5% (ideal); real engines achieve roughly half

workedExamples.q: An e-scooter uses 25 Wh/km. Electricity costs ₹8 per kWh. A petrol scooter does 50 km/l with petrol at ₹100/l. Compare cost per km.
workedExamples.answer: EV ≈ ₹0.20/km vs petrol ≈ ₹2/km — about one-tenth the energy cost

An engine gives 120 N·m into a gear pair with ratio 4 : 1 (output slower). Find the output torque and, if the input turns at 2,000 rpm, the output speed.

summary: Work = force × distance; power = work ÷ time; torque is turning force; P = τω.
Four-stroke petrol engines: intake, compression, power (spark), exhaust over two crank turns.
Cooling, lubrication, starter motors and fuel injection keep engines running; ideal petrol–air ratio ≈ 14.7 : 1.
Diesel engines compress air strongly so injected fuel self-ignites; higher efficiency and torque; turbochargers add air.
BS-VI norms require catalytic converters, particulate filters and SCR systems.
Heat engines are limited by Carnot: η ≤ 1 − T_cold/T_hot; real cars convert about 20–35% of fuel energy.
Gears trade speed for torque; clutch, CVT and differential match engine to wheels; EVs need one fixed gear.
A current in a magnetic field feels force F = BIL; this drives electric motors.
EV motors use a rotating field from three-phase stator coils: PMSM/BLDC or induction designs; 90–97% efficient.
EV system: battery, BMS, inverter, controller, reduction gear, charger; regenerative braking recovers energy.
Range ≈ kWh ÷ Wh/km; charging time ≈ energy ÷ charger power; heat and full/empty storage age batteries.
Hybrids, CNG, ethanol and hydrogen are other paths; EV emissions depend on electricity sources and battery production.

Ratio of cylinder volume before and after compression.

A circuit converting DC into AC.

rd-engineering-internet-packet.title: How the Internet Moves a Packet
rd-engineering-internet-packet.subtitle: Your WhatsApp message travels to Kolkata in a blink — chopped up, addressed, routed and reassembled

sections.h: A message's secret journey
sections.md:
Meera in Pune sends a photo of her new puppy to her cousin in Kolkata. Two ticks appear almost instantly. In that half-second the photo was **cut into hundreds of small pieces**, each stamped with addresses, launched through a Wi-Fi radio, carried along copper and glass fibre, passed hand to hand through a dozen machines called **routers**, possibly through an undersea cable to a data centre, and back — then glued together in the right order on her cousin's phone.

No single company owns the internet. No central computer directs the traffic. It is a **network of networks** — tens of thousands of independent networks (Jio, Airtel, BSNL, universities, Google, banks) that have agreed to speak the same languages, called **protocols**.

In this read we follow one packet:

1. Why the internet uses **packets** instead of a fixed line.
2. The **layers**: how jobs are divided like departments in a post office.
3. Your **home network**: MAC addresses, DHCP and the Wi-Fi router.
4. **IP addresses** and **DNS** — finding where to send.
5. **Routers** and how they choose a path.
6. **TCP**: making an unreliable network reliable.
7. The physical journey: Wi-Fi, fibre, undersea cables.
8. **Speed**: bandwidth, latency and content delivery networks.
9. **Encryption**: keeping the message private.

sections.h: Packets, not phone lines
sections.md:
Old telephone networks used **circuit switching**: when you called someone, the exchange connected a dedicated wire path from you to them for the whole call. Simple and steady — but wasteful. During pauses in conversation, that whole path sat idle and nobody else could use it.

The internet uses **packet switching**. Data is broken into chunks called **packets**, usually up to about 1,500 bytes. Each packet carries a **header** — like an envelope — with the source and destination addresses. Packets travel independently, sharing every link with packets from millions of other people. If one route is busy or broken, packets can go another way.

Think of moving a whole wedding party from Pune to Kolkata. Circuit switching is booking an entire private train. Packet switching is sending each guest by whichever scheduled train has a seat — they may take different routes, arrive in a different order, and the host counts them in at the other end.

Packet switching was developed in the 1960s, independently by Paul Baran in the USA and Donald Davies in the UK, and first used on the **ARPANET** in 1969. Its key advantage: the network keeps working even if parts fail, and links are used efficiently.

A 2 MB photo split into 1,400-byte data chunks makes about **1,430 packets**.

check.q: What is the main advantage of packet switching over circuit switching?
options: Links are shared efficiently and traffic can route around failures
check.why: Independent packets share every link and can take alternate paths, making the network efficient and resilient.

sections.h: Layers: the internet's division of labour
sections.md:
Sending a packet involves many jobs, so engineers split them into **layers**. Each layer does one job and relies on the layer below, a bit like India Post: you write a letter (content), put it in an envelope with a PIN code (addressing), the post office sorts it (routing), and a van or train physically carries it (transport medium). The writer does not care whether it goes by train or truck.

| Layer (TCP/IP model) | Job | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Application | what the data means | HTTPS, WhatsApp protocol, email (SMTP), DNS |
| Transport | end-to-end delivery between programs | TCP (reliable), UDP (fast, no guarantees), QUIC |
| Internet (network) | addressing and routing across networks | IP (IPv4, IPv6) |
| Link | one hop across one physical network | Wi-Fi, Ethernet, 4G/5G radio |
| Physical | bits as signals | radio waves, light in fibre, voltages on copper |

As data goes down the stack on the sender, each layer **wraps** it in its own header — **encapsulation**, like an envelope inside an envelope inside a parcel. At each router the outer link-layer envelope is opened and replaced for the next hop, but the IP envelope stays. At the receiver, layers **unwrap** in reverse.

Transport-layer headers also carry **port numbers**, which say *which program* on a computer should receive the data — 443 for HTTPS web traffic, 53 for DNS. The IP address finds the building; the port finds the flat.

> **Did you know?** The textbook OSI model has seven layers; the practical internet uses the simpler TCP/IP model shown here.

sections.h: Your home network: MAC addresses, DHCP and the Wi-Fi box
sections.md:
The journey starts in Meera's living room, at the small box with blinking lights that the broadband company installed. That box is really three devices in one: a **Wi-Fi access point** (the radio), a **switch** (connecting wired devices) and a **router** (connecting the home to the internet). With fibre-to-the-home it also contains an **ONT**, which turns light pulses in the fibre into electrical signals.

**MAC addresses.** Every network card — in a phone, laptop or smart TV — has a 48-bit hardware address burned in at the factory, written like `3C:22:FB:1A:09:7E`. The link layer uses MAC addresses to deliver a frame across *one* local network, such as from the phone to the Wi-Fi box. Think of it as a flat number inside one housing society: useful at the gate, meaningless in another city.

**DHCP.** When Meera's phone joins the Wi-Fi, it has no IP address yet. It broadcasts *Is there a DHCP server?* The router replies with an offer: a private IP address (say `192.168.1.7`), the router's own address (the **default gateway**), and which DNS resolver to use. The lease lasts some hours and is renewed automatically. This is why you never type addresses by hand.

**ARP.** To send a packet to the gateway, the phone needs the gateway's MAC address. It asks the whole local network, *Who has 192.168.1.1?* and the router answers with its MAC. Now the phone can wrap the IP packet in a Wi-Fi frame addressed to the router.

**Sharing the air.** Wi-Fi is a shared radio channel. Devices listen before talking and back off randomly if they collide, a bit like polite people in a meeting. Too many neighbours' networks on the same channel slow everyone down — which is why newer routers use the less crowded 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands.

> **Did you know?** Your phone shows 'connected, no internet' when DHCP and Wi-Fi worked but the router's link to the ISP is down — the first hop is fine, the rest of the journey is not.
keyTerms: MAC address — fixed hardware address used on one local network
DHCP — protocol that hands out IP addresses automatically
Default gateway — the router that carries packets out of the local network

check.q: What does DHCP give a phone that joins a Wi-Fi network?
options: An IP address, the gateway address and DNS server details
check.why: DHCP leases an IP address and tells the device its default gateway and DNS resolver, so it can start talking at once.

sections.h: Addresses: IP and the internet's phone book (DNS)
sections.md:
Every device on the internet needs an **IP address**. The older **IPv4** uses 32 bits, written as four numbers like `142.250.193.78`. That allows about 4.3 billion addresses — not enough for 8 billion people and their phones, laptops and smart bulbs. So:

- **IPv6** uses 128 bits (written like `2404:6800:4009:82b::200e`), giving about 3.4 × 10³⁸ addresses. India has been among the world's leading countries in IPv6 adoption, helped by large mobile networks.
- **NAT** (network address translation) lets your home router share one public IPv4 address among all your devices, which use private addresses like `192.168.1.5`.

Humans prefer names like `whatsapp.net`. The **Domain Name System (DNS)** converts names into IP addresses, like looking up a contact before dialling:

1. Your phone asks a **resolver** (run by your ISP, or a public one).
2. If the resolver does not have the answer cached, it asks a **root server**: who handles `.net`?
3. The `.net` server says which servers are **authoritative** for `whatsapp.net`.
4. That authoritative server returns the IP address.
5. The resolver caches the answer for a set time (the TTL), so the next lookup is instant.

All this often takes under 50 milliseconds — and usually happens from cache.

> **Did you know?** India's own `.in` and `.भारत` domains are managed by the National Internet Exchange of India (NIXI).
keyTerms: IP address — numeric address of a device on the internet
DNS — the system that translates names into IP addresses
NAT — sharing one public address among many private devices

check.q: Why was IPv6 introduced?
options: IPv4's 4.3 billion addresses are not enough for all devices
check.why: IPv4's 32-bit space ran out; IPv6's 128-bit addresses give an essentially unlimited supply.

sections.h: Routers: passing the parcel, hop by hop
sections.md:
A **router** is a computer specialised in one task: receive a packet, read its destination IP, decide which outgoing link brings it closer, send it on. It does this in microseconds, millions of times a second.

Each router keeps a **routing table**: a list of address ranges (prefixes) and the next hop for each. For example:

| Destination prefix | Send to |
|---|---|
| 49.36.0.0/14 | link to Jio network |
| 157.240.0.0/16 | link to Meta network |
| 0.0.0.0/0 (default) | upstream provider |

When several entries match, the router picks the **longest prefix** — the most specific match — like a postman who sorts first by state, then city, then street.

How do routers fill these tables? Inside one organisation, routers talk using protocols such as **OSPF**, which compute shortest paths across the network map. Between organisations, the **Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)** is used: each network (an *autonomous system*) announces which address ranges it can reach. BGP is as much about business agreements as geography.

Every IP packet also carries a **TTL (time to live)** counter. Each router reduces it by 1; if it hits 0, the packet is dropped. This stops a mistaken loop from circulating a packet forever. The tool `traceroute` uses TTL cleverly to list each router on a path.

Networks also meet at **Internet Exchange Points (IXPs)** — buildings where many networks connect directly. Exchanges in Mumbai, Delhi and Chennai keep Indian traffic inside India instead of detouring abroad.

check.q: Why does every IP packet carry a TTL counter?
options: So a packet caught in a routing loop is eventually discarded
To store the time of day
check.why: Each router decrements TTL; at zero the packet is dropped, so loops cannot circulate packets forever.

sections.h: TCP: reliability on top of chaos
sections.md:
IP makes a promise of **best effort** only. Packets may be lost (a congested router drops them), duplicated, corrupted or arrive out of order. Yet your photo arrives perfect. That is the job of **TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)**.

**1. Handshake.** Before sending data, the two ends agree to talk with a three-way handshake: SYN (let's talk), SYN-ACK (agreed), ACK (great). This sets up starting **sequence numbers**.

**2. Numbering.** Every byte gets a sequence number. If packets arrive out of order, the receiver sorts them.

**3. Acknowledgements.** The receiver sends ACKs saying *I have everything up to byte N*. If the sender does not hear an ACK within a timeout — or sees repeated ACKs for the same byte — it **retransmits**.

**4. Checksums.** Each segment has a checksum; corrupted segments are discarded and resent.

**5. Flow control.** The receiver advertises how much buffer space it has, so a fast server does not flood a slow phone.

**6. Congestion control.** TCP starts slowly and increases its sending rate until losses or delays suggest the network is full, then backs off. Millions of computers doing this independently is what stops the internet from jamming like Silk Board junction at 6 pm.

Not everything needs TCP's caution. Live video calls and online games often use **UDP**, which just sends — a late packet is useless anyway, so better to skip it than wait. Modern web traffic increasingly uses **QUIC**, which runs over UDP but builds in reliability and encryption with fewer round trips.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#111827'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' fill='#fff' text-anchor='middle'><text x='120' y='25'>Meera's phone</text><text x='480' y='25'>Server</text></g><line x1='120' y1='35' x2='120' y2='290' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='480' y1='35' x2='480' y2='290' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='3'/><g stroke-width='3' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13'><line x1='120' y1='50' x2='480' y2='90' stroke='#22c55e'><animate attributeName='stroke-dasharray' values='0 400;400 0' dur='1s' fill='freeze'/></line><text x='300' y='60' fill='#86efac' text-anchor='middle'>SYN</text><line x1='480' y1='100' x2='120' y2='140' stroke='#3b82f6'><animate attributeName='stroke-dasharray' values='0 400;0 400;400 0' dur='2s' fill='freeze'/></line><text x='300' y='112' fill='#93c5fd' text-anchor='middle'>SYN-ACK</text><line x1='120' y1='150' x2='480' y2='190' stroke='#22c55e'><animate attributeName='stroke-dasharray' values='0 400;0 400;0 400;400 0' dur='3s' fill='freeze'/></line><text x='300' y='162' fill='#86efac' text-anchor='middle'>ACK</text><line x1='120' y1='210' x2='480' y2='250' stroke='#f59e0b'><animate attributeName='stroke-dasharray' values='0 400;0 400;0 400;0 400;400 0' dur='4s' fill='freeze'/></line><text x='300' y='222' fill='#fcd34d' text-anchor='middle'>DATA (seq 1–1400)</text><line x1='480' y1='255' x2='120' y2='290' stroke='#a78bfa'><animate attributeName='stroke-dasharray' values='0 400;0 400;0 400;0 400;0 400;400 0' dur='5s' fill='freeze'/></line><text x='300' y='265' fill='#c4b5fd' text-anchor='middle'>ACK 1401</text></g></svg>
