rd-history-europeans-company.title: The Coming of the Europeans and the East India Company
rd-history-europeans-company.subtitle: How a trading company from a small island ended up ruling a subcontinent

sections.h: Pepper, ships and a sea route
sections.md:
In May **1498** three small Portuguese ships dropped anchor near **Calicut** (Kozhikode) on the Malabar coast. Their commander, **Vasco da Gama**, had sailed around the **Cape of Good Hope** in southern Africa, guided across the Arabian Sea by an experienced pilot from the East African coast. For the first time, Europeans had found a direct **sea route to India**.

Why did they want it so badly? **Spices** — pepper, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom — were enormously valuable in Europe for flavouring and preserving food and for medicines. So were India's fine **cotton and silk textiles**. Until then this trade passed through many hands — Indian, Arab, Persian and Venetian merchants — and each took a profit. A direct route promised huge gains.

The **Zamorin** (Samudri raja) of Calicut received da Gama, but Indian and Arab merchants were well established, and Indian buyers found Portuguese goods unimpressive. Still, da Gama returned with a cargo worth many times the cost of the voyage, and others followed.

Over the next 350 years, a trading enterprise from Britain would grow into the ruler of most of India. In this read we follow:

1. The Portuguese, Dutch, French and English arrive.
2. The East India Company sets up trade.
3. Trade turns to conflict: Bengal, Plassey and Buxar.
4. Company rule: Diwani, famine and reform.
5. Expansion: Mysore, the Marathas, Subsidiary Alliance, Doctrine of Lapse, Punjab.
6. Setting up a new administration and army.
7. Ruling the countryside: new revenue systems.
8. The impact on Indian society and economy.

check.q: Why did European traders want a direct sea route to India?
options: To buy spices and textiles directly and avoid middlemen's profits
check.why: Spices and textiles were extremely valuable; a direct route cut out many intermediaries and increased profits.

sections.h: Rivals on the waves: Portuguese, Dutch, French, English
sections.md:
**The Portuguese** were first. Under **Afonso de Albuquerque** they captured **Goa** in **1510**, which remained Portuguese until 1961. They tried to control sea trade by force, issuing passes (*cartazes*) to Asian ships and attacking those without them, and also set up posts at Daman, Diu and elsewhere.

**The Dutch** formed the **United East India Company (VOC)** in **1602**. They concentrated on the spice islands of Indonesia but also traded from Indian ports such as Pulicat and Nagapattinam, and in Bengal.

**The English East India Company** received a **charter** from **Queen Elizabeth I** on **31 December 1600**, granting it the sole right to trade with the East — no other English trading group could compete. It was a company of merchants who bought shares; profits were divided among them.

**The French** set up their company in **1664**, and established their main base at **Pondicherry** (Puducherry) in 1674.

The problem was that all these companies wanted the **same things** — fine cotton and silk, pepper, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon — and competition pushed up prices and cut profits. The only way the trading companies could flourish was by **eliminating rivals**. So the urge to secure markets led to fierce battles. Trade was carried on with **arms**, and trading posts were protected through **fortification**. This would soon draw the companies into Indian politics.

fig.caption: Europeans arrive

check.q: Why did rivalry among European companies lead to fighting?
options: They all wanted the same goods, so eliminating rivals was the way to profit
check.why: Competition for the same goods raised prices; companies used fortified posts and force to drive rivals out.

sections.h: The East India Company sets up trade
sections.md:
The English Company's first **factory** — a warehouse and office where traders worked, not a manufacturing plant — was set up on the banks of the **Tapti** at **Surat** in **1613**, after permission from Mughal emperor **Jahangir**. The ambassador **Sir Thomas Roe** visited Jahangir's court in 1615 to secure better terms.

The Company expanded:

- **Madras** — Fort St George, **1639**.
- **Bombay** — received by the English Crown as part of the dowry of the Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza (1661) and leased to the Company in 1668.
- **Calcutta** — in **1690**, a settlement was set up on the Hooghly; it grew around **Fort William**.

These three became the bases of the Company's later **Presidencies**: Bombay, Madras and Bengal.

In Bengal, the Company bribed and persuaded Mughal officials. In **1717**, the Mughal emperor **Farrukhsiyar** issued a **farman** (royal order) granting the Company the right to trade **duty-free**. But Company officials also carried on private trade, on which they were supposed to pay duty — and they refused. This caused an enormous loss of revenue for Bengal.

The Bengal Nawabs protested. **Murshid Quli Khan**, followed by **Alivardi Khan**, were strong Nawabs. They refused to grant the Company concessions, demanded large tributes for the right to trade, denied it any right to mint coins, and stopped it from extending its fortifications. They accused the Company of deceiving the government, harming the revenue and undermining the Nawab's authority. The Company, for its part, claimed that the demands of local officials were unjust and that trade could flourish only if duties were removed.
keyTerms: Factory — a trading post with warehouses and offices
Farman — a royal order
Presidency — an administrative unit based on Bombay, Madras or Calcutta

check.q: What did the farman of 1717 grant the Company?
check.why: Emperor Farrukhsiyar's farman allowed the Company to trade without paying duties, which officials then abused for private trade.

sections.h: From trade to wars: Plassey and Buxar
sections.md:
In **1756**, **Sirajuddaulah** became Nawab of Bengal after Alivardi Khan's death. The Company was worried about his power and supported a rival. Sirajuddaulah ordered the Company to stop meddling and to stop fortifying Calcutta. When it refused, he marched with 30,000 soldiers, captured the English factory at Kassimbazar and then **Fort William** in Calcutta.

The Company sent **Robert Clive** with troops from Madras. Negotiations failed. On **23 June 1757**, the two armies met at **Plassey** (Palashi). Sirajuddaulah lost — mainly because one of his commanders, **Mir Jafar**, kept his troops out of the fight. Clive had secretly promised to make Mir Jafar Nawab. The **Battle of Plassey** was the Company's first major victory in India, won as much through **conspiracy** as fighting.

The Company still did not want to rule directly; it wanted a puppet who would grant trade concessions. Mir Jafar was made Nawab but, when he protested, was replaced by **Mir Qasim**. When Mir Qasim in turn complained, he too was challenged. With the Mughal emperor **Shah Alam II** and the Nawab of **Awadh**, Mir Qasim fought the Company at **Buxar** in **1764** and was defeated. Mir Jafar was reinstated (and paid the Company huge sums).

Buxar was in some ways more decisive than Plassey: the Company defeated the combined forces of three Indian powers.

In **1765**, after Mir Jafar died, the Mughal emperor appointed the Company as the **Diwan** of the provinces of **Bengal, Bihar and Orissa** — giving it the right to collect revenue. This **Diwani** gave the Company control over vast resources. Now Bengal's revenue could finance Company purchases of cotton and silk, maintain its troops, and build forts — without bringing gold and silver from Britain.

check.q: What did the Diwani of 1765 give the Company?
options: The right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
check.why: As Diwan, the Company collected the land revenue of three provinces, financing its trade and army from Indian resources.

sections.h: Company rule in Bengal: plunder, famine and reform
sections.md:
After Plassey and the Diwani, Company officials grew rich. Many returned to Britain with fortunes and were mocked as **'nabobs'** (an English version of nawab). Clive himself was questioned by Parliament about his wealth.

The Company now had revenue but little idea of how to govern. The revenue demand stayed high, artisans were pressured to sell to the Company at low prices, and the economy suffered. In **1770**, a terrible **famine** struck Bengal; estimates suggest about **one-third** of the population of Bengal died. Contemporary and later historians link the scale of the disaster partly to harsh revenue collection and poor administration, as well as drought.

British Parliament began to regulate the Company:

- The **Regulating Act of 1773** set up a **Supreme Court** at Calcutta and a court of appeal; **Warren Hastings** became the first **Governor-General** (1773–1785), with powers over the Presidencies of Bombay and Madras.
- **Pitt's India Act of 1784** created a **Board of Control** in London to supervise the Company's political affairs.

The Company's official trade monopoly was ended in 1813 (except for trade in tea and with China, ended in 1833), and from then on the Company became mainly a **ruling body**.

check.q: What did the Regulating Act of 1773 do?
options: Set up a Supreme Court at Calcutta and created the post of Governor-General
check.why: The Act was Parliament's first attempt to regulate Company rule, establishing a Supreme Court and a Governor-General.

sections.h: Expansion: Mysore and the Marathas
sections.md:
From the 1770s, the Company followed a more aggressive policy of expansion.

**Mysore.** Under **Haidar Ali** (ruled 1761–1782) and his famous son **Tipu Sultan** (1782–1799), Mysore became powerful. It controlled the profitable trade of the Malabar coast. In **1785**, Tipu stopped the export of sandalwood, pepper and cardamom through the ports of his kingdom and disallowed local merchants from trading with the Company. He also built a modern army with French help and used **rockets** in battle. Four **Anglo-Mysore Wars** were fought (**1767–69, 1780–84, 1790–92 and 1799**). Only in the last — the **Battle of Seringapatam** (Srirangapatna) in **1799** — did the Company win; Tipu was killed defending his capital. Mysore was placed under the former ruling dynasty of the Wodeyars, with a subsidiary alliance.

**The Marathas.** After their defeat at the **third Battle of Panipat** in **1761** (against Ahmad Shah Abdali), the Marathas were divided into several states under chiefs (sardars) — the Sindhias, Holkars, Gaikwads and Bhonsles — loosely united under the **Peshwa** at Pune. The Company fought three **Anglo-Maratha Wars**:

- **First (1775–82)**: no clear winner; ended with the **Treaty of Salbai** (1782).
- **Second (1803–05)**: on different fronts; the British gained Orissa and territories north of the Yamuna, including Agra and Delhi.
- **Third (1817–19)**: crushed Maratha power. The Peshwa was removed and sent to Bithur near Kanpur with a pension. The Company now had complete control over territories south of the Vindhyas.

check.q: In which war and year was Tipu Sultan killed?
check.why: Tipu died defending Seringapatam in 1799, at the end of the fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

check.q: Under the Subsidiary Alliance, Indian rulers had to…
options: give up their own armed forces and pay for Company troops stationed with them
check.why: Rulers were 'protected' by Company troops they had to pay for, losing military independence.

sections.h: A new administration and army
sections.md:
The Company's territories were divided into administrative units called **Presidencies** — Bengal, Madras and Bombay — each ruled by a Governor, with the **Governor-General** at the top.

**Warren Hastings** introduced several reforms, especially in **justice**. From 1772, each district had two courts — a **criminal court (faujdari adalat)** and a **civil court (diwani adalat)**. European district **collectors** presided over civil courts, assisted by **maulvis** and Hindu **pandits** who interpreted Indian laws. Criminal courts were still under a qazi and a mufti, but supervised by collectors. Since Brahmin pandits gave different interpretations of the dharmashastras, a digest of Hindu laws was compiled in **1775**, and a code of Muslim laws by 1778. Under the Regulating Act, a **Supreme Court** was set up in Calcutta, and a **Sadar Nizamat Adalat** (court of appeal) also.

The principal figure in an Indian district was the **Collector**, whose main job was to collect revenue and taxes and maintain law and order with the help of judges, police officers and *darogas*. His office, the **Collectorate**, became the new centre of power and patronage.

**The army.** The Company recruited peasants into its army as **sepoys** (from *sipahi*, soldier), trained in European-style infantry discipline, drill and regulations. Cavalry declined as warfare changed to muskets and matchlocks. By 1820 the Company's army was one of the largest in Asia. In the early nineteenth century it also began developing a **uniform military culture**, which sometimes clashed with sepoys' caste and community sensibilities — another long-term cause of 1857.

check.q: Who was the principal Company official in a district?
check.why: The Collector collected revenue and kept order; the Collectorate became the centre of district power.

sections.h: Ruling the countryside: new revenue systems
sections.md:
Land revenue was the Company's main source of income, and it experimented with several systems.

**Permanent Settlement (1793).** Under **Lord Cornwallis**, in Bengal, **rajas and taluqdars were recognised as zamindars**. They were asked to collect rent from the peasants and pay revenue to the Company. The amount was **fixed permanently** — it would never be increased. The Company hoped this would ensure a regular flow of revenue and encourage zamindars to invest in improving land.

In practice, the revenue was fixed so high that many zamindars could not pay and **lost their estates**, which were auctioned. Later, when prices and cultivation rose, the Company could not claim more. Peasants found the system extremely oppressive: rents rose, they had no security, and they often had to borrow from moneylenders and lost land when they could not pay.

**Mahalwari Settlement (1822).** In the North Western Provinces, an Englishman named **Holt Mackenzie** devised this system. Collectors visited villages, inspected land, measured fields and recorded customs and rights. The estimated revenue of each plot was added up to calculate the revenue each village (**mahal**) had to pay. The demand was to be **revised periodically**. The village headman was responsible for collecting it.

**Ryotwari (Munro) System.** In the south, developed by Captain **Alexander Read** and **Thomas Munro**, the settlement was made **directly with the cultivators (ryots)**, who had tilled the land for generations. Their fields were carefully surveyed before the revenue assessment was made. Munro thought the British should act as paternal fathers protecting the ryots.

In all systems, the revenue demand was usually so high that peasants fled villages or fell into debt. Within a few decades, it was clear that the new systems were not working as officials had hoped.

left.title: Permanent Settlement (1793)
points: Zamindars lost estates when they could not pay
Peasants faced high rents and insecurity

right.title: Mahalwari (1822) & Ryotwari
points: Demand often too high, causing debt and flight

check.q: In the Ryotwari system, with whom did the Company settle revenue?
check.why: Munro's system made the settlement directly with the peasants who cultivated the land.

sections.h: Impact on India's economy and society
sections.md:
Company rule changed India deeply.

**Crops for Europe.** The British pushed cultivation of crops needed in Europe: **indigo** for dyeing, **opium** (exported to China), **jute**, **tea**, **sugar**, **wheat** and **cotton**. In Bengal, indigo planters forced ryots to grow indigo under unfair contracts; in **1859**, thousands of ryots refused — the **Indigo Rebellion (Nil Bidroha)**. The play *Neel Darpan* by Dinabandhu Mitra (1860) depicted their suffering. The government appointed an Indigo Commission, which found planters guilty of coercion.

**Crafts and trade.** Indian textiles had dominated world markets. But British machine-made cloth, protected in Britain by tariffs and later sold cheaply in India, undercut Indian weavers. Weaving centres such as Dhaka and Murshidabad declined. Many historians describe this as **deindustrialisation**, and nationalists later spoke of a **drain of wealth** from India to Britain — Dadabhai Naoroji developed this argument in the nineteenth century.

**New towns and institutions.** Bombay, Madras and Calcutta became great colonial cities. Courts, collectorates, survey offices, English education (after the 1830s) and later railways and the telegraph reshaped Indian life.

**Resistance.** From the start, Indians resisted — Sirajuddaulah, Tipu Sultan, the Marathas, Rani Channamma, tribal communities such as the Santhals (1855) and countless peasants. These struggles prepared the ground for the great **Uprising of 1857**, after which the Crown took over from the Company.

**How historians know:** Company records (they kept careful accounts, letters and reports), official surveys and censuses, Parliamentary inquiries, travellers' accounts, paintings by European artists, and Indian sources such as court chronicles, petitions and popular songs. Because so many records were produced by the rulers, historians read them critically and search for Indian voices.

check.q: What was the Indigo Rebellion of 1859?
options: A revolt of sepoys in Delhi
A refusal by Bengal ryots to grow indigo under unfair contracts
check.why: Bengal peasants refused to grow indigo for planters who forced them into unfair contracts, leading to an official inquiry.

summary: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498; Portuguese took Goa in 1510.
The English East India Company was chartered on 31 Dec 1600; Dutch VOC 1602; French company 1664.
Companies wanted the same goods, so they fought rivals and fortified posts.
English factories: Surat (1613), Madras (1639), Bombay (1668), Calcutta (1690).
Farrukhsiyar's farman (1717) allowed duty-free trade, which was abused; Bengal Nawabs protested.
Plassey (23 June 1757): Clive defeated Sirajuddaulah through Mir Jafar's betrayal; Buxar (1764) defeated three Indian powers.
The Diwani (1765) gave the Company revenue rights in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa; famine of 1770 followed.
Regulating Act (1773) and Pitt's India Act (1784) brought Parliament's control; Warren Hastings first Governor-General.
Four Anglo-Mysore wars ended with Tipu's death in 1799; three Anglo-Maratha wars ended Maratha power by 1819.
Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley), paramountcy (Hastings) and the Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie) expanded Company control; Awadh annexed 1856; Punjab 1849.
Administration: Presidencies, Collectors, new courts, a large sepoy army.
Revenue systems: Permanent Settlement (1793), Mahalwari (1822), Ryotwari (Munro); demands were often oppressive.
Impact: commercial crops (indigo, opium), decline of handicrafts, the drain of wealth, and growing resistance leading to 1857.

rd-history-gandhi-mass-movements.title: Gandhi and the Mass Movements, 1919–1947
rd-history-gandhi-mass-movements.subtitle: A handful of salt, a spinning wheel, and millions of people who refused to cooperate

sections.h: A pinch of salt at Dandi
sections.md:
On the morning of **6 April 1930**, on the beach at **Dandi** in Gujarat, a thin 60-year-old man in a dhoti bent down and picked up a lump of natural salt from the mud. With that small act, **Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi** broke the British **salt law**, which made it illegal for Indians to make or sell salt and let the government keep a monopoly and tax it.

Salt? Why salt? Because everyone — rich and poor, Hindu and Muslim, in every village — needed it. A tax on salt hurt the poorest most. By choosing salt, Gandhi turned an abstract demand for freedom into something every Indian could understand and act on. Within weeks, thousands across India were making salt, picketing shops and courting arrest.

This was Gandhi's genius: he turned the freedom struggle from a movement of educated professionals into a **mass movement** of peasants, workers, women, students and traders. In this read we follow:

1. Gandhi's ideas and early campaigns in India.
2. The Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh.
3. Khilafat and Non-Cooperation (1920–22).
4. The 1920s: Swarajists, Simon Commission, revolutionaries.
5. Purna Swaraj and the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34).
6. Round Table Conferences, Poona Pact and the 1935 Act.
7. War, Quit India (1942) and Subhas Chandra Bose.
8. The road to independence and Partition (1945–47).
9. How different people experienced the movement — and how historians see it.

check.q: Why did Gandhi choose salt as the symbol of Civil Disobedience?
options: Salt was only used by the rich
Every Indian needed salt, and the tax hurt the poor most, so it united everyone
Salt was made only in Britain
check.why: Salt was a universal necessity; the salt tax and monopoly symbolised British injustice in a way all could feel.

sections.h: Gandhi's ideas and first experiments
sections.md:
Gandhi had spent about two decades in **South Africa**, where he fought racist laws against Indians using a new method he called **satyagraha** — 'insistence on truth' or 'truth-force'. He returned to India in **January 1915**.

**Satyagraha** meant:

- if the cause was true and the struggle was against injustice, physical force was not needed;
- without seeking vengeance or being aggressive, a satyagrahi could win the battle through **non-violence** (*ahimsa*), by appealing to the conscience of the oppressor;
- people — including the oppressors — had to be persuaded to see the truth, not forced.

Gandhi tried this method in three local struggles:

- **Champaran (Bihar), 1917**: he went to support peasants forced by European planters to grow indigo under the oppressive *tinkathia* system.
- **Kheda (Gujarat), 1918**: he supported peasants who could not pay land revenue because of crop failure and a plague epidemic, and demanded that revenue collection be relaxed.
- **Ahmedabad, 1918**: he organised a satyagraha among **cotton mill workers** for higher wages, and went on a fast.

These campaigns made Gandhi known as a leader who went to the people, lived simply and fought for their concrete grievances. They also brought in a generation of new leaders — such as **Rajendra Prasad** in Champaran and **Vallabhbhai Patel** in Kheda.
keyTerms: Satyagraha — non-violent resistance based on truth
Ahimsa — non-violence
Tinkathia — system forcing peasants to grow indigo on part of their land

check.q: Where did Gandhi lead a satyagraha for indigo peasants in 1917?
check.why: In Champaran, Bihar, Gandhi supported peasants oppressed by European indigo planters.

sections.h: Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh, 1919
sections.md:
In **1919**, the government passed the **Rowlatt Act** despite united opposition by Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council. It gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed **detention of political prisoners without trial for two years**.

Gandhi called for a nationwide **satyagraha** against these 'unjust laws'. It began with a **hartal** (strike) on **6 April 1919**. Rallies were held in towns, workers went on strike, and shops closed. Alarmed, the British arrested local leaders in Amritsar and barred Gandhi from entering Delhi.

On **13 April 1919**, the day of **Baisakhi**, a large crowd gathered in the enclosed ground of **Jallianwala Bagh** in **Amritsar**. Some had come to protest the repression, others to attend the fair; many were unaware that martial law had been imposed. **General Reginald Dyer** blocked the exit points and ordered his troops to open fire on the crowd. Official figures said 379 people were killed; Indian estimates were much higher, and over a thousand were wounded. Dyer later said his object was to 'produce a moral effect' — to create fear in the minds of satyagrahis.

The massacre caused nationwide outrage. **Rabindranath Tagore** returned his knighthood in protest. Crowds took to the streets in many towns; the government responded with brutal repression — people were humiliated, forced to crawl on the streets, villages were bombed. Seeing violence spread, Gandhi called off the movement. But Jallianwala Bagh had destroyed many Indians' faith in British justice.

fig.caption: The Gandhian era at a glance

check.q: What did the Rowlatt Act allow?
options: Detention of political prisoners without trial for up to two years
The end of the salt tax
check.why: The Rowlatt Act gave the government sweeping powers to imprison political activists without trial.

sections.h: Khilafat and Non-Cooperation, 1920–22
sections.md:
After the First World War, the defeated **Ottoman** Sultan of Turkey — regarded by many Muslims as the **Khalifa** (spiritual head) — faced a harsh peace treaty. To defend the Khalifa's powers, a **Khilafat Committee** was formed in Bombay in March 1919, led by brothers **Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali** along with **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad** and others.

Gandhi saw a chance to bring Hindus and Muslims together in a unified national movement. At the Calcutta session of the Congress in **September 1920**, he convinced other leaders to start a **Non-Cooperation Movement** in support of Khilafat as well as for **swaraj**. The Nagpur session in December 1920 confirmed it.

In his famous book **Hind Swaraj** (1909), Gandhi had declared that British rule was established in India with the cooperation of Indians and survived only because of this cooperation. If Indians refused to cooperate, British rule would collapse within a year.

The movement proposed stages:

- surrender of titles awarded by the government;
- **boycott** of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and **foreign goods**;
- a full civil disobedience campaign if the government persisted.

In towns, thousands of students left government schools and colleges, headmasters and teachers resigned, and lawyers gave up practice. Council elections were boycotted in most provinces. Foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires; the import of foreign cloth **halved between 1921 and 1922**. Merchants refused to trade in foreign goods. People wore **khadi** (hand-spun cloth), and the **charkha** (spinning wheel) became a symbol.

In the countryside, the movement took different forms (see later). Then, in **February 1922**, at **Chauri Chaura** in Gorakhpur district (UP), a peaceful demonstration turned into a violent clash with the police, and a police station was set on fire, killing several policemen. Gandhi felt the movement was turning violent and that satyagrahis needed proper training. He **withdrew** the Non-Cooperation Movement. Many leaders were disappointed.

check.q: Why did Gandhi withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922?
options: Because of violence at Chauri Chaura, which he felt went against non-violence
Because the British asked him to
Because the Khilafat had been restored
check.why: After the police station at Chauri Chaura was burnt and policemen killed, Gandhi called off the movement to uphold non-violence.

sections.h: Different strands in the movement
sections.md:
Each social group joined with its own hopes, and interpreted *swaraj* in its own way.

**Peasants in Awadh.** Led by **Baba Ramchandra**, a sanyasi who had earlier worked as an indentured labourer in Fiji, peasants protested against talukdars and landlords who demanded very high rents and many other cesses, and made them do *begar* (forced labour). They demanded reduction of revenue, abolition of begar and social boycott of oppressive landlords. In **1920**, **Jawaharlal Nehru** toured Awadh villages, and the **Oudh Kisan Sabha** was set up. In some places, people attacked the houses of talukdars and merchants, believing Gandhi had declared that no taxes need be paid — showing how Gandhi's name was understood differently from his intent.

**Tribal peasants of the Gudem Hills (Andhra Pradesh).** In the early 1920s, the colonial government had closed large forest areas, preventing people from grazing cattle or collecting fuelwood and fruits. **Alluri Sitarama Raju** led a militant guerrilla movement. He was inspired by the Non-Cooperation Movement but argued that India could be liberated only by the use of force. He was captured and executed in **1924**.

**Plantation workers in Assam.** Under the **Inland Emigration Act of 1859**, plantation workers were not permitted to leave the tea gardens without permission. When they heard of the movement, thousands defied the authorities and left for home, believing that 'Gandhi Raj' was coming. They were caught by the police and brutally beaten.

**Businessmen** supported the boycott of foreign goods (they wanted protection against imports), though they were wary of militancy. **Industrial workers** joined in some places, but the Congress was reluctant to include workers' demands for fear of alienating industrialists.

check.q: Who led a militant tribal movement in the Gudem Hills?
check.why: Alluri Sitarama Raju led a guerrilla struggle in the Gudem Hills against forest restrictions, and was executed in 1924.

sections.h: The late 1920s: Swarajists, Simon and revolutionaries
sections.md:
After Non-Cooperation ended, some leaders were tired of mass struggles and wanted to participate in elections to the provincial councils set up by the Government of India Act of 1919. **C. R. Das** and **Motilal Nehru** formed the **Swaraj Party** within the Congress (1923) to argue for a return to council politics. Younger leaders like **Jawaharlal Nehru** and **Subhas Chandra Bose** pressed for more radical mass agitation and full independence.

In **1927–28**, the British government in Britain set up a statutory commission under **Sir John Simon** to look into the functioning of the constitutional system in India and suggest changes. The problem was that it **did not have a single Indian member**. When it arrived in **1928**, it was greeted with the slogan **'Go back, Simon'**. All parties, including the Congress and the Muslim League, joined in the protest. In **Lahore**, the police lathi-charged a protest led by **Lala Lajpat Rai**, who died of his injuries soon after.

Also in **1928**, **Vallabhbhai Patel** led a successful peasant campaign in **Bardoli** (Gujarat) against enhanced land revenue — it earned him the title *Sardar*.

**Revolutionaries.** A group of young people, including **Bhagat Singh**, **Chandrashekhar Azad**, **Sukhdev** and **Rajguru**, believed in revolutionary action to end British rule. They formed the **Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA)** in 1928. In **April 1929**, Bhagat Singh and **Batukeshwar Dutt** threw harmless bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi, shouting 'Inquilab Zindabad', and courted arrest to spread their message. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged on **23 March 1931**, becoming national heroes. Gandhi disagreed with their methods, but many young Indians were inspired by their courage.

check.q: Why was the Simon Commission boycotted?
options: It wanted to end British rule
check.why: An all-British commission deciding India's constitutional future was an insult, so Indians protested with 'Go back, Simon'.

sections.h: Purna Swaraj and the Civil Disobedience Movement
sections.md:
At its **Lahore session in December 1929**, presided over by **Jawaharlal Nehru**, the Congress formalised the demand of **'Purna Swaraj'** — complete independence. It was declared that **26 January 1930** would be celebrated as Independence Day, when people were to take a pledge to struggle for complete independence.

Gandhi needed a way to make this abstract idea concrete. On **31 January 1930** he sent a letter to Viceroy **Irwin** with **eleven demands** — some of general interest, others specific to different classes, from industrialists to peasants — so that all classes could identify with them. The most stirring was the demand to **abolish the salt tax**. If the demands were not met by 11 March, the Congress would launch civil disobedience.

Irwin was unwilling to negotiate. So on **12 March 1930**, Gandhi started his famous **Salt March** with **78** trusted volunteers from his **Sabarmati Ashram** to the coastal town of **Dandi**, about 240 miles (around 385 km) away, walking about 10 miles a day for **24 days**. Thousands came to hear him. On **6 April** he ceremonially violated the law, manufacturing salt by boiling sea water.

This marked the start of the **Civil Disobedience Movement**. Now people were asked not only to refuse cooperation, but also to **break colonial laws**. Across the country, thousands broke the salt law and demonstrated in front of government salt factories. Foreign cloth was boycotted; liquor shops were picketed. Peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari taxes; village officials resigned; forest people violated forest laws.

**Women** participated in large numbers — marching, manufacturing salt, picketing. At **Dharasana** salt works, **Sarojini Naidu** led satyagrahis who were beaten by police, and the American journalist Webb Miller's report shocked the world. In the North-West Frontier, **Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan** — the 'Frontier Gandhi' — led the non-violent **Khudai Khidmatgars**; when he was arrested in 1930, angry crowds in Peshawar faced armoured cars and police firing.

The government responded with brutal repression, arresting around **100,000** people. In **March 1931**, Gandhi signed the **Gandhi–Irwin Pact**: he agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London, and the government agreed to release political prisoners.

check.q: How was the Civil Disobedience Movement different from Non-Cooperation?
options: People were asked not only to refuse cooperation but to break colonial laws
It was led by the Muslim League
check.why: Civil Disobedience went further by asking people to deliberately break laws such as the salt law.

sections.h: Round Table Conferences, the Poona Pact and the 1935 Act
sections.md:
In **December 1931**, Gandhi went to London for the **Second Round Table Conference**, but the negotiations broke down, especially over the representation of minorities. He returned disappointed. Back in India, the government had begun a new cycle of repression; Gandhi relaunched Civil Disobedience, which continued for over a year but lost momentum by **1934**.

**Dalits and the Poona Pact.** Dalit leaders, especially **Dr B. R. Ambedkar**, who organised the Dalits into the Depressed Classes Association in 1930, demanded **separate electorates** that would choose Dalit members for legislative councils. Ambedkar clashed with Gandhi at the Second Round Table Conference. When the British government granted separate electorates for the Depressed Classes (the Communal Award, 1932), Gandhi began a **fast unto death**, believing separate electorates would slow their integration into society. Ambedkar ultimately accepted Gandhi's position, and the **Poona Pact** of **September 1932** gave the Depressed Classes (later Scheduled Castes) **reserved seats** in provincial and central legislative councils, but to be voted for by the **general electorate**.

**Muslims.** After Non-Cooperation, many Muslims felt alienated from the Congress, as communal tensions grew. Efforts at a common understanding failed; at the All Parties Conference in 1928, disagreements over reserved seats and representation could not be resolved. Large sections of Muslims were lukewarm towards Civil Disobedience.

**The Government of India Act, 1935** introduced **provincial autonomy**. In the **1937** elections, the Congress formed governments in most provinces (it resigned in 1939 when Britain declared India a party to the Second World War without consulting Indians).

check.q: What did the Poona Pact of 1932 provide?
options: Reserved seats for the Depressed Classes, elected by the general electorate
check.why: After Gandhi's fast, Ambedkar and Gandhi agreed on reserved seats for Dalits within joint electorates.

sections.h: War, Quit India and Subhas Chandra Bose
sections.md:
When the **Second World War** began in **1939**, the Viceroy declared India at war without consulting Indian leaders. Congress ministries resigned. In **March 1940**, the **Muslim League** passed the **Lahore Resolution**, demanding 'independent states' for Muslims in the north-western and eastern areas — the basis of the demand for **Pakistan**.

In **1942**, Britain sent **Sir Stafford Cripps** with proposals for dominion status after the war; the Congress rejected them as inadequate. Gandhi then decided to launch a final movement. On **8 August 1942**, at the Gowalia Tank Maidan in **Bombay**, the Congress passed the **Quit India** resolution. Gandhi gave the call: **'Do or die'** — Indians should either free India or die in the attempt.

The very next morning, Gandhi and other leaders were **arrested**. Yet the movement spread, led by younger leaders and ordinary people — students, workers, peasants. Many attacked symbols of British authority: railway stations, police stations, telegraph lines. In some places — **Satara** in Maharashtra, **Medinipur** in Bengal, **Ballia** in UP — people set up **parallel governments**. **Aruna Asaf Ali** hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank; **Usha Mehta** ran an underground radio. The British used massive force; by the end of 1943 over **90,000** people were arrested and around 1,000 killed in police firing. The movement was suppressed, but it showed that Britain could not govern India for much longer against such widespread opposition.

**Subhas Chandra Bose**, a radical Congress leader who had been president in 1938 and 1939, believed in more militant methods. He escaped house arrest in 1941, sought help from Germany and later Japan, and in Southeast Asia led the **Azad Hind Fauj** (**Indian National Army, INA**), formed from Indian prisoners of war and civilians, with the slogan 'Dilli Chalo'. The INA fought alongside Japanese forces on the India–Burma border in 1944 but was forced back. Bose is believed to have died in an air crash in **1945**, though some still debate this. The **INA trials** at Delhi's Red Fort in **1945–46** caused nationwide protests and sympathy for the soldiers.

check.q: What was Gandhi's call during the Quit India Movement?
check.why: On 8 August 1942 Gandhi called on Indians to 'do or die' — to free India or perish in the attempt.

sections.h: The road to freedom and Partition, 1945–47
sections.md:
After the war, Britain was exhausted, and the mood in India was charged. In **February 1946**, ratings (sailors) of the **Royal Indian Navy** mutinied in Bombay and other ports, supported by strikes in the city. Britain's new Labour government decided to transfer power.

The **Cabinet Mission (1946)** proposed a loose federation that would keep India united, with provinces grouped regionally. The Congress and Muslim League could not agree. The League called for **'Direct Action'** on **16 August 1946** to press its demand for Pakistan; terrible communal riots broke out in **Calcutta**, then in Noakhali, Bihar, and elsewhere. Gandhi walked through riot-hit Noakhali, trying to restore peace.

The new Viceroy, **Lord Mountbatten**, announced the **3 June 1947** plan for **Partition**. On **14–15 August 1947**, Pakistan and India became independent. Gandhi did not celebrate; on 15 August he was in Calcutta, fasting and praying for peace amid the violence.

**How historians see the Gandhian movements.** Historians agree that Gandhi transformed nationalism into a mass movement and gave it a powerful moral language. They also note that:

- people joined for many reasons and understood 'swaraj' in their own ways;
- the movement included many strands — moderates, revolutionaries, socialists, Bose's INA, peasant, worker, tribal and Dalit movements;
- tensions over caste and religion were never fully resolved, and the end of the struggle came with Partition's tragedy.

Sources include Gandhi's own writings (*Hind Swaraj*, *Young India*, *Harijan*, his autobiography *The Story of My Experiments with Truth*), police and intelligence reports, newspapers, letters, photographs and oral histories of ordinary participants.

check.q: What happened on 16 August 1946?
options: The Muslim League's Direct Action Day, followed by riots in Calcutta
The Quit India resolution was passed
check.why: The League's call for Direct Action led to severe communal violence in Calcutta and beyond.

summary: Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 with the method of satyagraha — non-violent resistance through truth.
Early campaigns: Champaran (1917), Kheda (1918), Ahmedabad mill workers (1918).
The Rowlatt Act (1919) led to a nationwide hartal; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) shocked India.
Khilafat and Non-Cooperation (1920–22): boycott of schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth; khadi and the charkha.
Peasants (Awadh, Baba Ramchandra), tribals (Alluri Sitarama Raju) and Assam plantation workers joined in their own ways.
Chauri Chaura (Feb 1922) led Gandhi to withdraw the movement.
1920s: Swaraj Party; Simon Commission boycotted (1928); Lajpat Rai's death; Bardoli; Bhagat Singh and the HSRA.
Lahore Congress (Dec 1929) declared Purna Swaraj; 26 Jan 1930 celebrated as Independence Day.
Dandi March (12 Mar–6 Apr 1930) launched Civil Disobedience: breaking laws, boycotts, women's participation, Khudai Khidmatgars.
Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931); Second Round Table Conference; Poona Pact (1932); Government of India Act (1935).
Quit India (8 Aug 1942): 'Do or die'; leaders arrested; parallel governments; mass repression.
Subhas Chandra Bose led the INA; the INA trials and RIN mutiny (1946) stirred India.
Cabinet Mission failed; Direct Action Day riots; the 3 June plan led to independence and Partition on 15 August 1947.

rd-history-harappan.title: The Harappan Civilisation
rd-history-harappan.subtitle: Planned cities, silent seals and a script nobody can read

sections.h: A city under a railway line
sections.md:
In the 1850s, engineers building a railway between Lahore and Multan needed bricks for the track bed. Near the village of **Harappa** they found mounds full of beautifully baked old bricks, and carted many away. Nobody guessed that those bricks were about four and a half thousand years old.

Seventy years later, in **1921**, **Daya Ram Sahni** began excavating at Harappa, and in **1922** **R. D. Banerji** dug at **Mohenjodaro** in Sindh. In **1924**, **John Marshall**, Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, announced to the world that a new civilisation had been discovered — as old as those of Egypt and Mesopotamia.

We call it the **Harappan Civilisation** (after the first site found) or the **Indus Valley Civilisation**. But it stretched far beyond the Indus: from Afghanistan to Gujarat, from Balochistan to Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. More than a thousand sites are known.

In this read we explore:

1. When it flourished and where.
2. How its cities were planned — citadels, drains, houses, the Great Bath.
3. What people ate and how they farmed.
4. Crafts: beads, shell, metal, pottery — and how archaeologists identify craft centres.
5. Trade within the subcontinent and with distant lands.
6. Seals, script, weights and measures.
7. Who ruled? Social differences and burials.
8. The mystery of the decline.
9. How archaeologists reconstruct the past — and the debates.

check.q: Why is it called the 'Harappan' civilisation?
options: Because it was ruled by King Harappa
Because Harappa was the first site of this civilisation to be discovered
Because all sites are in Harappa
check.why: Archaeologists often name a culture after the first site where its remains were found — here, Harappa.

sections.h: When and where
sections.md:
Archaeologists use the term **culture** for a group of objects, distinctive in style, usually found together within a specific geographical area and period. The Harappan culture is identified by distinctive objects — **seals, beads, weights, stone blades** and even **baked bricks** of standard size.

The civilisation is usually dated in phases:

| Phase | Approximate dates |
|---|---|
| Early Harappan | before c. 2600 BCE |
| **Mature Harappan** (the great cities) | c. **2600 – 1900 BCE** |
| Late Harappan | after c. 1900 BCE |

The early cultures of the region were agricultural and pastoral, with small villages — such as **Mehrgarh** in Balochistan, where farming began several thousand years earlier. The Mature Harappan phase saw the growth of large cities.

Main sites:

- **Harappa** (Punjab, Pakistan) and **Mohenjodaro** (Sindh, Pakistan) — the largest cities.
- **Kalibangan** (Rajasthan), on the dry bed of the Ghaggar.
- **Lothal** (Gujarat), near the Sabarmati and the Gulf of Khambhat.
- **Dholavira** (Gujarat), on Khadir Bet island in the Rann of Kutch — a World Heritage Site since 2021.
- **Rakhigarhi** and **Banawali** (Haryana); **Ropar** (Punjab); **Chanhudaro** (Sindh); **Kot Diji**; **Shortughai** (far north in Afghanistan); **Nageshwar** and **Balakot** on the coast.

Many sites lie along the **Indus** and its tributaries, and along the **Ghaggar–Hakra** channel, which carried more water then than it does today.

check.why: The Mature Harappan phase, when cities like Mohenjodaro flourished, dates to about 2600–1900 BCE.

sections.h: Planned cities: citadel and lower town
sections.md:
The most unique feature of the Harappan civilisation was the development of **urban centres**. Let us look at **Mohenjodaro**, the best-known.

The settlement was divided into two sections:

- the **Citadel** — smaller but higher, built on mud-brick platforms and walled. It had buildings that were probably used for special public purposes, such as the **warehouse** (earlier called the 'granary') and the **Great Bath**.
- the **Lower Town** — larger but lower, also walled, where most people lived.

Several buildings were built on **platforms**, which served as foundations. It has been calculated that if one labourer moved roughly one cubic metre of earth daily, just to put the foundations in place would have required **four million person-days** — in other words, mammoth labour, organised on a large scale. The settlement was **first planned** and then built: the platforms were laid first, and then the town was built on them within a fixed area.

Bricks — sun-dried or baked — were of a **standardised ratio**: the length and breadth were four times and twice the height respectively (**4 : 2 : 1**). Such bricks were used at all Harappan settlements.

**Roads and drains.** Streets were laid out in an approximate **grid** pattern, intersecting at right angles. It seems that streets with drains were laid out first and then houses built along them. If domestic waste water had to flow into the street drains, every house needed at least one wall along a street. Drains were covered with bricks or stone slabs; some had **inspection holes** for cleaning. Large drains even had **soak pits** (sumps). Mackay, an archaeologist, wrote that this was 'certainly the most complete ancient system as yet discovered'.

**Dholavira** was different: it was divided into **three parts** (citadel, middle town and lower town), each walled, with huge stone-cut **water reservoirs** to collect rain — a vital need in arid Kutch. A large inscription of Harappan signs, sometimes called a 'signboard', was found near a gateway. **Lothal** had a large basin some archaeologists interpret as a **dockyard**, though others think it was a water tank; the debate continues.

check.q: What does the standard 4 : 2 : 1 brick ratio across many sites suggest?
options: Some common standards or coordination existed across a wide area
check.why: The same brick proportions at sites hundreds of kilometres apart point to shared standards and coordination.

sections.h: Houses and the Great Bath
sections.md:
**Domestic architecture.** The Lower Town at Mohenjodaro gives examples of residential buildings. Many were centred on a **courtyard**, with rooms on all sides. The courtyard was probably the centre of activities such as cooking and weaving, particularly in hot and dry weather.

There was an apparent concern for **privacy**: there are no windows in the walls along the ground level, and the main entrance does not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard. Every house had its own **bathroom**, paved with bricks, with drains connected through the wall to the street drains. Some houses have remains of **staircases** to reach a second storey or the roof. Many houses had **wells**, often in a room that could be reached from outside and perhaps used by passers-by. Scholars have estimated that Mohenjodaro had about **700 wells**.

**The Great Bath** is a large rectangular tank in a courtyard on the Citadel, surrounded by a corridor on all four sides. It is about **12 m long, 7 m wide and 2.4 m deep**. There were two flights of steps on the north and south leading into the tank, which was made **watertight** by setting bricks on edge and using a mortar of **gypsum**, with a layer of bitumen. There were rooms on three sides, in one of which was a large well. Water from the tank flowed into a huge drain. Across a lane to the north lay a smaller building with eight bathrooms.

Scholars suggest that the uniqueness of the structure, along with its location on the Citadel, indicates that it was meant for some kind of special **ritual bath** — though we cannot be sure.

options: With bricks set on edge, gypsum mortar and a layer of bitumen

sections.h: Food and farming
sections.md:
Harappans ate a wide range of plant and animal products, including fish. Archaeologists reconstruct diets from **charred grains and seeds**, studied by **archaeo-botanists**.

- **Grains**: **wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame**. **Millets** are found at sites in Gujarat. Finds of **rice** are relatively rare.
- **Animal bones**: cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig. Studies by **archaeo-zoologists** indicate these animals were domesticated. Bones of wild species such as boar, deer and gharial are also found; we do not know whether Harappans hunted them or got the meat from other hunting communities. Bones of fish and fowl also occur.
- **Cotton** was grown; pieces of woven cotton cloth have survived at Mohenjodaro wrapped around objects.

**Agricultural technologies.** Representations on seals and terracotta sculpture show that the **bull** was known, and archaeologists infer that oxen were used for ploughing. Terracotta **models of the plough** have been found at sites in **Cholistan** and at **Banawali** (Haryana). Archaeologists have found evidence of a **ploughed field at Kalibangan**, associated with Early Harappan levels. The field had two sets of furrows at right angles to each other, suggesting that **two different crops were grown together**.

As most Harappan sites lie in semi-arid lands, **irrigation** was probably needed. Traces of **canals** have been found at **Shortughai** in Afghanistan (though not in Punjab or Sindh), and water reservoirs at **Dholavira** may have stored water for agriculture. **Wells** were also likely used.

Tools for harvesting are less clear: did farmers use stone blades set in wooden handles, or metal tools? Archaeologists are still finding out.

check.q: What does the ploughed field at Kalibangan with furrows at right angles suggest?
options: Two different crops were grown together
check.why: Two sets of furrows crossing each other indicate a practice of growing two crops in the same field.

sections.h: Crafts: beads, shell, metal and pottery
sections.md:
**Chanhudaro**, a tiny settlement (less than 7 hectares) compared with Mohenjodaro (125 hectares), was almost exclusively devoted to **craft production**: bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making.

**Beads** were made of a remarkable variety of materials: **carnelian** (a beautiful red stone), **jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite**; metals like **copper, bronze and gold**; and **shell, faience and terracotta** (burnt clay). Some were made of two or more stones cemented together, some of stone with gold caps. Shapes included disc-shaped, cylindrical, spherical, barrel-shaped and segmented. Some were decorated by **incising or painting**, and some had designs etched onto them.

Techniques varied with the material. **Steatite**, a very soft stone, was easily worked; some beads were moulded out of a paste made with steatite powder. The red colour of **carnelian** was obtained by **firing** the yellowish raw material and the beads at various stages. Nodules were chipped into rough shapes and then finely flaked into the final form. **Grinding, polishing and drilling** completed the process. Specialised drills have been found at Chanhudaro, **Lothal** and more recently Dholavira.

**Shell** objects — bangles, ladles, inlay — were made at **Nageshwar** and **Balakot**, both near the coast. These were taken to other settlements.

**Metal**: copper and bronze were used for tools, weapons, ornaments and vessels; gold and silver for ornaments and vessels. The famous **bronze 'dancing girl'** from Mohenjodaro shows skill in casting.

**Pottery**: wheel-made red pottery painted with black designs is typical of Harappan sites.

**How do archaeologists identify craft centres?** They look for **raw materials** such as stone nodules, whole shells and copper ore; **tools**; **unfinished objects**; and **rejects and waste material** — waste is one of the best indicators of craft work. Sometimes larger waste pieces were used to make smaller objects, showing that, apart from small specialised centres, craft production was also undertaken in large cities like Mohenjodaro and Harappa.

check.q: Which is the best indicator of a craft production centre?
options: Waste material, unfinished objects and raw materials
check.why: Debris, rejects and unfinished items show that objects were actually being made at a place.

sections.h: Trade near and far
sections.md:
Many materials Harappans used were not available locally. Archaeologists think Harappans used several strategies to procure them:

- **Settlements** were established where raw materials were available: **Nageshwar** and **Balakot** for shell, **Shortughai** in distant Afghanistan near the best source of **lapis lazuli** (a blue stone that was highly valued), and **Lothal** near sources of carnelian (from Bharuch in Gujarat), steatite (from south Rajasthan and north Gujarat) and metal (from Rajasthan).
- **Expeditions** were sent to areas such as the **Khetri** region of Rajasthan (for copper) and south India (for gold). These expeditions established communication with local communities. Finds of Harappan artefacts in these areas are indications of such contacts. In the Khetri area, archaeologists have found evidence of what they call the **Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture**, with distinctive non-Harappan pottery and an unusual wealth of copper objects — possibly supplying copper to the Harappans.

**Contact with distant lands.** Copper was also probably brought from **Oman**, on the south-eastern tip of the Arabian peninsula. Chemical analyses have shown that both Omani copper and Harappan artefacts have traces of **nickel**, suggesting a common origin. A distinctive type of Harappan vessel, a large jar coated with a thick layer of black clay, has been found at Omani sites.

**Mesopotamian texts** from the third millennium BCE mention contact with regions named **Dilmun** (probably the island of **Bahrain**), **Magan** (probably **Oman**) and **Meluhha** (possibly the **Harappan region**). They mention products from Meluhha: **carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold and varieties of wood**. A Mesopotamian myth says of Meluhha: 'May your bird be the *haja*-bird', which some scholars identify as the peacock. Harappan seals, weights, dice and beads have been found in Mesopotamia. Communication with Oman, Bahrain or Mesopotamia was probably by **sea**; Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha as a land of seafarers, and seals show ships and boats.

fig.caption: Where Harappan raw materials came from

check.q: What name do Mesopotamian texts probably use for the Harappan region?
check.why: Mesopotamian records mention Meluhha, a land of seafarers supplying carnelian, lapis and copper — likely the Harappan region.

sections.h: Seals, script, weights and measures
sections.md:
**Seals and sealings** were used to facilitate long-distance communication. Imagine a bag of goods being sent from one place to another. Its mouth was tied with rope, and on the knot was affixed some wet clay on which one or more seals were pressed. If the bag reached with its **sealing intact**, it meant it had not been tampered with. The sealing also conveyed the identity of the sender.

The Harappan seal is possibly the civilisation's most distinctive artefact. Made of **steatite**, seals often contain **animal motifs** — the 'unicorn' (a one-horned animal), bull, elephant, tiger, rhinoceros — and signs from a script that remains **undeciphered**. One famous seal shows a figure seated cross-legged in a yogic posture surrounded by animals; some early archaeologists called it 'proto-Shiva', but many scholars caution against such identifications.

**The script.** Harappan seals usually have a line of writing, probably containing the name and title of the owner. Most inscriptions are **short**, the longest containing about **26 signs**. The script was **not alphabetical** (where each sign stands for a vowel or consonant): it had too many signs, somewhere between **375 and 400**. It was apparently written from **right to left**, as some seals show wider spacing on the right and cramping on the left. Writing has been found on a variety of objects: seals, copper tools, rims of jars, copper and terracotta tablets, jewellery, bone rods and even the ancient 'signboard'. Many scholars have tried, but no one has convincingly deciphered it.

**Weights.** Exchanges were regulated by a precise system of weights, usually made of a stone called **chert** and generally **cubical**, with no markings. The lower denominations were **binary** (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, etc., up to 12,800), while the higher followed the **decimal** system. Smaller weights were probably used for weighing jewellery and beads. Metal scale-pans have also been found.

check.q: Why do scholars think the Harappan script was not alphabetical?
options: It had about 375–400 signs, far too many for an alphabet
check.why: An alphabet has a small number of signs; with roughly 400 signs, the Harappan script must have worked differently.

sections.h: Who ruled? Social differences and burials
sections.md:
Archaeologists use certain strategies to find out whether there were **social or economic differences** among people.

**Burials.** At Harappan sites, the dead were generally laid in **pits**. Sometimes the pit was lined with bricks. Some graves contain **pottery and ornaments**, perhaps indicating a belief that these could be used in the afterlife. Jewellery has been found in burials of both men and women. In some instances, the dead were buried with **copper mirrors**. A necklace of shell rings, jasper and micro beads was found in one burial. But on the whole, the Harappans **did not believe in burying precious things with the dead** — unlike, say, the pharaohs of Egypt.

**Luxuries.** Archaeologists classify artefacts as **utilitarian** (objects of daily use like querns and pottery, made of ordinary materials) or **luxuries** (rare objects made from costly, non-local materials or with complicated technologies). Little pots of **faience** (a material made of ground sand or silica mixed with colour and gum and then fired), probably used as perfume bottles, were found mostly in large settlements like Mohenjodaro and Harappa, and were rare in small settlements like Kalibangan. Gold, too, was rare and precious: all the gold jewellery found at Harappan sites was recovered from **hoards**.

**Rulers?** Some archaeologists think Harappan society had **no rulers** and everybody enjoyed equal status. Others think there was **no single ruler but several** — Mohenjodaro had a separate ruler, Harappa another, and so on. Yet others argue that there was a **single state**, given the similarity in artefacts, the evidence for planned settlements, the standardised ratio of brick size, and the establishment of settlements near sources of raw material. A large building at Mohenjodaro was labelled a **'palace'** by archaeologists, but no spectacular finds were associated with it. A stone statue was labelled and is still known as the **'priest-king'**, because archaeologists were familiar with Mesopotamian history and its priest-kings — but the evidence for ritual practices is not clear. As of now, the last theory seems the most plausible to many, but it is still debated.

**Religion.** Many female figurines of terracotta, heavily jewelled, were found; some were regarded as **mother goddesses**. Stone statues of men in a seated posture, structures interpreted as **fire altars** at Kalibangan and Lothal, and seals showing ritual scenes suggest religious beliefs, but reconstructing Harappan religion remains largely speculative.

check.q: Why is the label 'priest-king' for a Mohenjodaro statue questioned?
options: Because it was based on Mesopotamian parallels, and evidence for Harappan priest-kings is unclear
Because it was found in Egypt
Because it is made of gold
check.why: Archaeologists borrowed the term from Mesopotamian history; Harappan evidence for such rulers or rituals is not clear.

sections.h: The end of the cities
sections.md:
By about **1800–1900 BCE**, most of the Mature Harappan sites in regions such as Cholistan had been **abandoned**. Simultaneously, there was an expansion of population into new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

In the few Harappan sites that continued to be occupied after 1900 BCE, there appears to have been a transformation of material culture: the **disappearance** of the distinctive artefacts of the civilisation — weights, seals, special beads; writing, long-distance trade and craft specialisation also disappeared. In general, far fewer materials were used. House construction techniques deteriorated and large public structures were no longer produced. Overall, artefacts and settlements indicate a **rural way of life** in what are called **'Late Harappan'** or **'successor cultures'**.

What brought about these changes? Several explanations have been put forward. These range from **climatic change**, **deforestation**, **excessive floods**, the **shifting and/or drying up of rivers**, to **overuse of the landscape**. Some of these 'causes' may hold for certain settlements, but they do not explain the collapse of the entire civilisation. It appears that a strong **unifying element**, perhaps the Harappan state, came to an end, as evidenced by the disappearance of seals, the script, distinctive beads and pottery, the shift from a standardised weight system to local weights, and the decline and abandonment of cities.

**The 'invasion' theory.** Archaeologist **Mortimer Wheeler** once suggested that Mohenjodaro was destroyed by invaders, citing groups of skeletons found in the upper levels. Later, **George Dales** and others showed that these skeletons did **not belong to the same period** and there was no evidence of a massacre. Most scholars today reject the idea of a sudden destruction by invaders.

check.q: What happened to Harappan culture after about 1900 BCE?
options: Many cities were abandoned and a simpler rural way of life replaced distinctive urban features
check.why: Seals, script, standard weights and planned cities disappeared, and Late Harappan cultures were largely rural.

sections.h: How archaeologists piece it together
sections.md:
Unlike later periods, we cannot read Harappan texts. So everything we know comes from **material remains** — and from the way archaeologists **interpret** them.

**Discovery story.** Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the ASI in the nineteenth century, visited Harappa but did not realise how old it was; he was more interested in sites mentioned by Chinese Buddhist pilgrims. Later, **seals** found at Harappa by Daya Ram Sahni and similar seals at Mohenjodaro helped show that these sites belonged to one archaeological culture. Marshall's announcement in 1924 changed world history.

**Methods.** Excavation was once done in arbitrary horizontal units, ignoring the **stratigraphy** (layers) of the site. Later archaeologists like **R. E. M. Wheeler** stressed following the stratigraphy, as different layers belong to different periods. After Partition (1947), Indian archaeologists located many sites in India, and new techniques followed: scientific dating, analysis of plant and animal remains, chemical tests on metals (like the nickel traces linking Oman copper), and studies of the ancient environment.

**Classifying finds.** Archaeologists classify finds by **material** (stone, clay, metal, bone, ivory) and by **function** — whether an object was a tool, ornament, or ritual object. Sometimes they work out function by comparing with present-day objects (such as querns, beads or stone blades) or with the context in which objects were found — in a house, a drain, a grave, a kiln.

**Problems of interpretation.** Religious practices are the hardest to reconstruct. Archaeologists often identify as 'ritual' anything unusual or unfamiliar. Some features are read by working back from later traditions — a practice called 'reading history backwards' — which can be useful but risky. Each new excavation, for example at **Rakhigarhi**, adds evidence and revises old ideas. The Harappans' silence makes them one of the greatest mysteries — and adventures — of history.

check.q: Why did Wheeler emphasise following stratigraphy in excavations?
options: Because different layers of a site belong to different periods, so mixing them confuses the evidence
Because it was required by Britain
check.why: Digging by natural layers keeps objects from different periods separate, giving accurate chronology.

summary: Harappa was excavated by Daya Ram Sahni (1921), Mohenjodaro by R. D. Banerji (1922); John Marshall announced the civilisation in 1924.
Mature Harappan phase: c. 2600–1900 BCE; sites from Afghanistan to Gujarat, Haryana and western UP.
Cities had a raised Citadel and a larger Lower Town, built on platforms after planning.
Bricks followed a 4 : 2 : 1 ratio; streets in a grid; covered drains with inspection holes.
Houses had courtyards, bathrooms, wells and privacy; Mohenjodaro had about 700 wells.
The Great Bath (about 12 m × 7 m × 2.4 m) was watertight and probably for ritual bathing.
Crops: wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea, sesame, millets; cotton; domestic animals; plough models; Kalibangan ploughed field; canals at Shortughai.
Crafts: beads (carnelian, steatite, faience), shell (Nageshwar, Balakot), metal, pottery; Chanhudaro was a craft centre.
Raw materials came from Shortughai, Khetri, Gujarat, south India; trade with Oman, Bahrain (Dilmun) and Mesopotamia (Meluhha).
Seals of steatite carry animals and an undeciphered right-to-left script of about 375–400 signs.
Chert cubical weights followed binary then decimal systems.
Burials and luxuries show some social differences; scholars debate whether there were rulers or a single state.
Cities declined around 1900 BCE; causes debated; the invasion theory is largely rejected.

rd-history-how-historians-know.title: How Historians Know the Past
rd-history-how-historians-know.subtitle: Detectives of time: coins, pots, palm leaves and potsherds that speak

sections.h: A mystery in a field
sections.md:
Imagine a farmer near a village in Uttar Pradesh ploughing after the monsoon. His blade strikes something hard. He digs, and out comes a clay pot full of small, greenish-black discs. They are coins, worn smooth, stamped with a king's face and letters nobody in the village can read.

What happens next is the heart of history. Under India's **Treasure Trove Act of 1878**, such finds must be reported to the government. Experts from a museum or the **Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)** arrive. A **numismatist** (coin expert) cleans the coins and reads the letters — perhaps Brahmi script, naming a Kushana king of about 1,900 years ago. Suddenly a quiet field becomes a clue: there was trade here, money, a ruler whose name reached this village.

Historians are detectives of time. They cannot visit the past, so they collect **evidence** — called **sources** — question it, compare it and build the most likely account. This read explains:

1. What history is and why we study it.
2. Dates, eras and counting time.
3. Kinds of sources: manuscripts, inscriptions, archaeology, coins.
4. Archaeology: digging, layers and dating.
5. Reading scripts and deciphering languages.
6. Oral traditions and the voices of ordinary people.
7. Sources for medieval and modern India: chronicles, paper, archives, newspapers, photographs.
8. Thinking like a historian: bias, comparison and debate.

check.q: What is a numismatist?
options: A person who reads inscriptions on stone
check.why: Numismatics is the study of coins; numismatists identify rulers, dates, metals and trade from them.

sections.h: What is history, and why does it matter?
sections.md:
**History** is the study of the past using evidence. It asks not only *what* happened but *how* and *why*, and *how we know*. It is about kings and battles, yes — but also about what people ate, the clothes they wore, the work they did, the games they played, what they believed, the songs they sang and how their societies changed.

Why study it?

- To understand how today's world came to be — our languages, festivals, cities, borders, laws.
- To learn how people solved (or failed to solve) problems.
- To understand people different from ourselves, and to develop **judgement**: weighing evidence, spotting exaggeration and propaganda.

The subcontinent has many names in the past. The word **India** comes from the **Indus** river, called **Sindhu** in Sanskrit. The Iranians and the Greeks, who came through the north-west about 2,500 years ago and were familiar with the Indus, called it the *Hindos* or *Indos*, and the land east of the river was called India. The name **Bharata** was used for a group of people who lived in the north-west and who are mentioned in the **Rigveda**, the earliest composition in Sanskrit (dated to about 3,500 years ago); later it was used for the country.

History is also never finished. New discoveries — a new excavation, a deciphered inscription, a forgotten letter in an archive — can change what we know.

check.q: From which river does the name 'India' come?
check.why: Iranians and Greeks called the Indus 'Hindos' or 'Indos', and the land beyond it India.

sections.h: Counting time: dates, BCE and CE
sections.md:
To put events in order, historians need **dates**. Today we commonly use a system that counts years from the traditional date of the birth of Jesus Christ.

- **CE** (Common Era) — years after that point; also written **AD** (*Anno Domini*, 'in the year of the Lord').
- **BCE** (Before Common Era) — years before it; also written **BC** ('Before Christ').

BCE years count **backwards**: 500 BCE is earlier than 400 BCE. So the Buddha (around the 6th–5th century BCE) lived before Ashoka (3rd century BCE).

A few other terms:

- **BP** — Before Present (used by scientists, 'present' being taken as 1950).
- A **century** is 100 years; the **first century CE** is years 1–100, so the **twenty-first century** is 2001–2100.
- A **millennium** is 1,000 years.
- **c.** (circa) means 'about'.

India has also used many other calendars: the **Vikram Samvat** (beginning 57 BCE), the **Shaka Samvat** (beginning 78 CE — the basis of India's **national calendar**), the Islamic **Hijri** calendar (beginning 622 CE), and many regional calendars. Inscriptions often give dates in these eras, so historians must convert them.

> **Try it:** How many years passed between 326 BCE (Alexander in the north-west) and 1526 CE (the first battle of Panipat)? Add the two: 326 + 1,526 − 1 = 1,851 years (we subtract 1 because there is no year 0).

check.q: Which is earlier: 300 BCE or 200 BCE?
check.why: BCE years count backwards, so 300 BCE is 100 years before 200 BCE.

sections.h: Manuscripts: books written by hand
sections.md:
Long before printing, books were **written by hand**. These are called **manuscripts** (from the Latin *manu*, 'hand'). In India they were usually written on **palm leaf** or on the specially prepared **bark of the birch** tree (*bhurja*), which grows in the Himalayas; later, from about the thirteenth century onwards, on **paper**.

Over the years, many manuscripts were eaten by insects, damaged by damp or destroyed, but many survive, often preserved in **temples, monasteries and libraries**. They deal with all kinds of subjects: **religious beliefs and practices, the lives of kings, medicine, science, poetry, plays and grammar**. They were written in **Sanskrit**, **Prakrit** (languages used by ordinary people) and **Tamil**, and later in Persian, Arabic and many regional languages.

**Problems with manuscripts.** Before printing, every copy was made by hand by a **scribe**. Scribes sometimes made small mistakes — a word here, a sentence there — or deliberately 'improved' a text. Over centuries, copies of the same text could become quite different. Historians compare different manuscripts of a text to try to guess what the original said. For example, the fourteenth-century chronicler **Ziyauddin Barani** wrote his chronicle first in 1356 and another version two years later; the two differ, and historians did not know about the first until the 1960s, when it was found among a large library collection.

Some texts were not written down at all for centuries: the **Vedas** were composed and **memorised** and passed down orally with extraordinary precision before being written.
keyTerms: Manuscript — a handwritten book
Scribe — a person who copied manuscripts
Prakrit — languages used by ordinary people in ancient India

check.q: Why do different copies of the same manuscript sometimes differ?
options: Because scribes copying by hand made changes or errors over centuries
Because the original authors wrote many different books
Because manuscripts were written in code
check.why: Each hand copy could introduce small changes, so historians compare manuscripts to reconstruct the original.

sections.h: Inscriptions: writing on hard surfaces
sections.md:
**Inscriptions** are writings on relatively hard surfaces such as **stone or metal**. Kings who wanted their orders to be known — or their victories remembered — had them inscribed. Other people also left inscriptions: merchants, monks, women who made gifts to temples.

The most famous early inscriptions in India are those of the Mauryan emperor **Ashoka** (3rd century BCE), carved on rocks and polished stone **pillars** across the subcontinent. Most are in **Prakrit**, written in the **Brahmi** script; in the north-west some are in **Kharosthi**, and a few in **Greek and Aramaic**. In them Ashoka speaks of his remorse after the **Kalinga war** and his policy of **dhamma**.

Other important kinds:

- **Prashastis** — praise-poems for kings, like the **Allahabad pillar inscription** of Samudragupta (4th century CE), composed by his court poet **Harishena**, or the **Aihole inscription** of Pulakeshin II.
- **Land grants** on **copper plates**, recording gifts of land to Brahmins, temples or monasteries.
- **Temple inscriptions**, like the Chola records of taxes and village assemblies at Uttaramerur.

**Strengths:** inscriptions are usually **contemporary** — written at the time — and permanent, so they are less likely to be altered than manuscripts.

**Limits:** letters may be faint or damaged; words may be hard to understand; and inscriptions reflect the **viewpoint** of the person who commissioned them. A king's inscription rarely mentions his defeats. Historians call the study of inscriptions **epigraphy**, and its specialists **epigraphists**.

check.q: Why must historians read a king's prashasti carefully?
options: Because it presents the king's own viewpoint and may exaggerate
Because it is written in English
check.why: Prashastis were written to glorify rulers, so historians check their claims against other evidence.

sections.h: Archaeology: reading the ground
sections.md:
Many people in the past did not write, and much of what they made has long since perished. **Archaeology** is the study of the past through **material remains**: buildings made of stone and brick, paintings and sculpture, tools, weapons, pots, pans, ornaments, coins, bones of animals, seeds and burnt grain.

Archaeologists **explore and excavate** — dig under the surface of the earth. When people live at a place for centuries, layers of debris build up: floors, walls, ash, broken pottery. Over time, a settlement becomes a **mound**. The deepest layers are usually the **oldest**, and the topmost the most recent — a principle called **stratigraphy**. By carefully recording which objects lie in which **layer**, archaeologists can work out the sequence of life at the site.

**What can remains tell us?**

- **Bones** of animals show what people ate and which animals they kept (**archaeo-zoology**).
- **Charred grains and seeds** show which crops were grown (**archaeo-botany**).
- **Tools and waste** reveal crafts — a heap of shell fragments with unfinished bangles shows a workshop.
- **Pottery styles** help date layers and show contact between regions.
- **Burials** and luxury objects hint at beliefs and social differences.

Archaeologists also use **surveys** — walking across landscapes, studying satellite images and aerial photographs, and using ground-penetrating radar — to find sites without digging everywhere. Excavation destroys the layers as it digs, so careful **recording**, drawings and photographs are essential.
