sections.h: Looking back: what had changed by 1919?
sections.md:
Compare 1885 and 1919 and the change is striking.

- **Who took part.** In 1885 a few dozen educated men met in a college hall. By 1919 shopkeepers, students, mill workers, peasants and women were joining hartals across the country.
- **What was demanded.** From more seats on councils, to *swaraj*, to Home Rule; the British themselves now spoke of 'responsible government'.
- **Methods.** Petitions gave way to boycott, swadeshi, mass meetings, festivals, revolutionary action and finally Gandhian satyagraha.
- **Women.** Women boycotted foreign goods in their kitchens, spun, joined processions in the Swadeshi years and led Home Rule work — Annie Besant became the first woman president of the Congress (1917). **Sarojini Naidu**, poet and orator, was rising as a leader.
- **Divisions.** Separate electorates and the founding of the Muslim League created a new line of division even as the Lucknow Pact showed cooperation was possible.

The British had used both concessions (reforms of 1892, 1909, 1919) and repression (sedition trials, press laws, Rowlatt). Historians often call this the policy of the **carrot and stick**.

> Did you know? *Vande Mataram*, from Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's novel *Anandamath* (1882), became the great slogan of the Swadeshi years; the British tried to ban its shouting in public.

check.q: Who was the first woman president of the Indian National Congress?
check.why: Annie Besant presided over the Calcutta session of 1917, the first woman to do so; Sarojini Naidu followed in 1925.

parts.md:
Calcutta, August 1905. Fourteen-year-old Nirmala watched her elder brother Ashok tip a bundle of cloth from his shoulder onto the heap in the middle of the square. Mill-made dhotis from Manchester, a shawl, a pair of foreign shoes, even a tin of imported biscuits. The crowd cheered. Someone struck a match, and the flames climbed into the humid evening sky while a group of students began to sing *Vande Mataram*.

Nirmala had brought nothing. Her mother had refused to part with her one good imported sari, saying it had cost too much. Nirmala felt ashamed — and then angry at herself for feeling ashamed.

At home that night her grandmother called her into the back room. On the floor sat an old wooden *charkha*, dusty from years of disuse. 'Before the mills,' her grandmother said, 'every house in our village spun. Burning cloth is easy. Making it is harder.' She showed Nirmala how to pull a thread from a cotton roll, how to turn the wheel steadily so the yarn did not snap.

The next weeks were full of small decisions. Her father, a clerk, began buying salt from an Indian merchant who charged a little more. Ashok's college friends opened a swadeshi store selling soap made in Bengal. Her mother joined women from the lane who promised not to buy foreign bangles. On 16 October, the day the partition began, the whole family fasted, and Nirmala tied a yellow thread rakhi on the wrist of the Muslim boy who sold vegetables at their gate, as Tagore had asked people to do.

Not everyone in their neighbourhood agreed. A shopkeeper grumbled that swadeshi cloth was coarse and expensive; a cousin in East Bengal wrote that many peasants there did not feel the movement was theirs. Nirmala listened to all of it. Six years later, when news came from the Delhi Durbar that the partition had been cancelled, she was twenty, and her own spun yarn had been woven into a plain white sari. She wore it to the celebration.

Nirmala's family is imagined, but every event around them — the bonfires, the rakhis, the swadeshi stores, the doubts of peasants, the 1911 annulment — is drawn from what historians know of the Swadeshi movement.

summary: The INC was founded in Bombay in December 1885 with 72 delegates; W. C. Bonnerjee presided.
Earlier associations, the press and grievances (Arms Act, Vernacular Press Act, Ilbert Bill) prepared the ground.
The 'safety valve' theory of Hume's role is now seen as too simple.
Moderates used petitions and argued the economic drain theory (Naoroji, R. C. Dutt).
Curzon partitioned Bengal on 16 October 1905, sparking the Swadeshi movement.
Swadeshi included boycott, Indian industries, national education and samitis.
Extremists (Lal–Bal–Pal, Aurobindo) demanded swaraj; Congress split at Surat in 1907.
The Muslim League was founded at Dacca in 1906; Morley–Minto (1909) gave separate electorates.
Partition of Bengal was annulled in 1911; capital moved to Delhi.
Home Rule Leagues (Tilak, Besant) and the Lucknow Pact came in 1916.
Gandhi developed satyagraha in South Africa and led Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad and Kheda (1918).
The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy; the Rowlatt Act allowed detention without trial.
Jallianwala Bagh massacre, 13 April 1919, transformed national feeling.
